{Null_Results} Text Messages Reveal OHS Director Hand-Picked Which Families to Receive Housing
As part of Nashville’s “Non-Traditional Rapid Rehousing” aka "MRRF", Office of Homeless Services Director Calvin had the final say of who was promised "a year of free housing" and a voucher.

Rich Text
Nov 10, 2025
∙ Paid
Text messages that were shared with me between Director Calvin and her staff from Aug 3, 2024 demonstrating her sharing confidential HMIS documents and making ad hoc housing placements decisions.

On Saturday morning, August 3, 2024, Nashville’s Office of Homeless Services Director April Calvin texted her staff to personally select which unhoused families would receive housing—reviewing confidential case records via text message, removing families from consideration based on their size, and coordinating placements outside the city’s federally mandated Coordinated Entry system that exists precisely to prevent this kind of ad hoc decision-making.

Recent reporting on Nashville’s Office of Homeless Services has revealed what appears to be a housing program launched with minimal public notice in summer 2024, relocating unhoused families into housing units under what’s classified in the fiscal year 2026 budget as “non-traditional rapid rehousing.”
Reports are this program may also be referred to going forward as “Metro Rapid Response Funds” or “MRRF.”
A line item from OHS’ ledger book with the memo line “OHS NOV 2024 RENT” billed to “Hillside Crossing LLC”.
The accounting string notes that it was billed against the ARPA Fund 30216, in a business unit related to RS2024-490 which allocated OHS ARPA Funds for Strobel House.

The program appears to trace back to placements beginning at least in summer and fall of 2024, when no fewer than eight families were placed into housing under the direct coordination of OHS Director April Calvin and the Nashville Rescue Mission.
Leases were drawn up under Metro supervision, and rent began being paid using ARPA funds that do not appear to have been obligated for such purposes.
Calvin’s response to my inquiry regarding why these families were still receiving eviction notices, over a month after I had brought this issue to the attention of Calvin and the Mayor’s Office.
The families were taken from the Nashville Rescue Mission and placed into housing units at two locations: 3230 Clarksville Pike and 717 Spence Lane.

Families were shuttled over to the properties and told they would receive a year of paid rent and housing vouchers for participating in the program, according to two families interviewed and a case manager with an organization responsible for providing support services to these families.
If you’re not already subscribed for this investigation or this Substack and want to see all the relevant content, choose one of these options below.
An Extraordinary Claim Requires Documentation

These are extraordinary claims: that the department in charge of a federally mandated program designed to provide equitable access to scarce housing resources (Coordinated Entry (CE)) has its director making these life-altering decisions outside of any recognized best practices.

1
A claim like that is nothing I would post on my Substack without documentation.
It is a claim I’m sure the Nashville Scene would never make without seeing evidence of this.
So now I would like you to be able to see what we’ve seen.
The Text Messages

Below are screenshots of a text thread conversation Director Calvin had in August of 2024, wherein she was texting with her OHS staff, sending them confidential HMIS documents with private unique identifiers visible even in the unredacted screenshots.

Evident in these messages is Director Calvin deciding which particular families will be receiving promises of a year of free housing and a housing voucher—promises that, notably, none of the families fully received.
All were told that their promised year of paid rent was being withdrawn, and eventually received eviction notices as OHS stopped paying their rent.
And at least two families did not receive the promised vouchers that OHS incentivized them with to leave the Rescue Mission.

On Saturday, August 3, 2024, at 7:31 AM, Calvin texted her staff:
“Ladies we are reducing our number to 8 smaller families that Ohs will house from the Mission due to the properties that are available.
“The 8 families will be housed at two different hotel conversions.
“[OHS employee name redacted] please select the families that have smaller kids or smaller family size.”

Calvin then reviewed individual HMIS records showing family details, including names, HMIS numbers, number of children, income sources (SSI/SSDI), and other personal information—all shared via text message.
After reviewing one family’s information, Calvin wrote: “I only saw one family with 3 kids Let’s remove them from the list and...”
The staff member responded that she would “do this and send out the notification and will call [case manager for Nashville Rescue Mission].”
Another asked about mobility accommodations for the ground-floor units.
Later that same day, Calvin wrote: “The next referral to advocate for on the case coordination meeting,” referring to another family.
A staff member noted one individual “May have trouble with stairs.
That’s the only mobility problem.”
Calvin responded with approval, noting she would ensure this person received a ground-floor unit.
The staff member then messaged: “Not that I am aware of.
[case manager for Nashville Rescue Mission] would have mentioned that, but I will double check.”
After another staff member asked for clarification, the response came: “Oh - sorry, yes - it is [case manager for Nashville Rescue Mission].
Can I give her your phone number?”

By the end of the exchange, Calvin had personally reviewed and approved which families would receive housing, which would be removed from consideration, and sent the final list to property management with instructions to prepare lease agreements for Monday, August 5, 2024.
These families entered into contracts with a landlord, being told OHS would be paying their rent for a year.
Metro chose the families, the landlords, and arranged the leases.
But by April, they were reneging on their promise and eviction notices starting showing up.
Despite coordinating all aspects of this process, Metro and OHS appear nowhere on these leases.

WHEREAS, more than 110 individuals and families served by PSH programs are at high risk of losing their housing; and

Dec 19, 2025

In 2025, {Rich Text} published 186,261 words across 94 posts—almost exactly the length of The Fellowship of the Ring (187,790 words), and in the same neighborhood as Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire .
That’s roughly 310 single pages, or about 510 words per day, every day, for a year.
Stacked against traditional journalism, it’s over 230 standard newspaper articles, produced without an editor, a newsroom, or a salary.
The average post ran just over 2,000 words—longer than most op-eds, shorter than most people’s patience for local government accountability reporting.
All of it written in coffee shops, Switchyards, at my kitchen table, and far too often at 2 AM on my couch when a public records request finally came through.
Below is a note from me about this past year.
Scroll past that and you can find all articles I published this year organized by topic.
Many are series that are best read in the sequences provided.
What 2025 Has Meant for Me
2025 has been…
a year.
It started off inauspiciously.
On New Years Day 2025, I was in Mexico City with my partner and friends and I got food poisoning.

I was sick enough that I had to be hospitalized and given an IV. A doctor later had to visit our AirBNB and administer another IV.
A week later there was an electrical fire in an office shed in the backyard of the home we rent.
I had been using it as my home office and storage for my decades worth of videography equipment, books I've collected, hardware tools, comic books — all the physical stuff that made me me.
I lost virtually all my personal possessions, besides my clothes and computer, in the fire.
And then there was everything going on in our country and city.
It’s been…
a year.
I’ve certainly been in some sort of fight or flight mode.
My anxiety found an outlet through my fingers onto a keyboard.
I disappeared into this work no one assigned to me.
I thank my partner for being patient and supportive in this year of deep fixation.
I would not be who I am without you.
I love you.
In 2025, I made some incredible friends.
I’ve been part of a movement.
Several movements.
I’ve been entrenched in the perennial push-and-pull of collectivist power vs elite capture of our society in a way I’ve aspired to but could never have been prepared for.
I have felt fully swept up in the moment.
I’ve been interviewed for television, news articles and podcasts.
I won an award.
And I got a piece of journalism I wrote actually edited, fact checked, and published by a media outlet I’ve long respected.
I made plenty of mistakes.
An incalculable number of tpyos.
Given public comment at innumerable council meetings.
Published financial records of city departments, helped make the case for internal audits.
Got my work called “fake news” and “misinformation” by city leaders but helped the truth prevail nonetheless.
I connected with the least and most powerful in our city (and often made the latter very upset with me).
The adage of journalism, comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable — I’ve come to know that vibe very well.
I’ve fought alongside people from all walks of life for change and reform, and more than once we got some good results.
The folks reading this, we’ve done so much together this year.
This will be a year I will never forget.
In some ways I am very ready for it to go away.
But it’s a year I’ll never fully let go.
There was piece of advice given to me early this year from someone who was not pleased with what I was writing.
He told me something to the effect of: “people who are becoming civically engaged should be careful in how they interact with bureaucrats.
Many young people who want change can be off putting when their thinking is too critical and they’re very strong minded.”
It was an honor to be offered advice from someone from such a high position of authority in our city.
And also to be called a young person still at 35.
But I haven’t taken his advice.
I’ve chosen not to lessen my critical thinking and to be more weak minded.
I’ve leaned in to my neuroatypicality and my ADHD and my special interests.
I have learned lessons about being more patient.
About holding my tongue and staying professional, even if it’s abundantly clear what I really think.
Not because it’s always wrong to be brash, but because it can sometimes be more effective to not say the quiet part out loud.
But there are also times where that is what is required.
In 2025, I found a role for myself in Nashville.
I think it’s something we all crave, to feel like we have a purpose.
I was most uncomfortable this year when I actually “broke news.”
I felt most in the pocket when I said what many people knew but were afraid to say.
Every time I posted this year, I never did it with the expectation that I had to do it again.
I let myself be fully guided by my impulses.
I had no publishing schedule, and never an outline of what I wanted to talk about.
Any structure to my articles or series I made was developed on the fly.
At times I worked with others to time things to other events.
Sometimes I collaborated with other writers.
But I always gave myself the option to walk away immediately from this Substack if it didn’t feel right.
And there were times where I thought “I’m done.”
Sometimes it was out of anxiety over the impact of what I was writing.
It is stressful to be worried if you're wrong about something important no one else is talking about.
It's even more stressful to worry that you are, in fact, very right about something important no one else is talking about.
Other times I thought of quitting it was out of boredom with being so damn serious.
But I kept coming back.
I don’t know who I’ll be in 2026.
Maybe I’ll be the same but more, or less, or maybe something entirely different and I’ll lose the support of the subscribers that like what they saw.
We’ll see.
I love that people have chosen to support this work with donations.
And that support is just cresting into an amount that actually might impact my tax returns and that is amazing.
But part of what has made these 186k words possible is not caring about any of that — so if in 2026 I’m not who you want me to be because of who I was in 2025, I’m sorry.
But know that central to what made me who you wanted this year was that I was not trying to be that at all.
But in 2025, I’ve been honored to be your Metro Watchdog.
Woof woof.

-Mike

Nashville Department of Emergency Communications Director Stephen Martini has been placed on administrative leave pending disciplinary action following an outside investigation into his management of the department.
“Today, I received a report outlining serious factual findings substantiated against Director Steve Martini and the functions he oversees,” Mayor Freddie O’Connell said in a release.
“I asked for his resignation and he declined.
He has been placed on administrative leave pending disciplinary action, and we will commence the formal disciplinary process immediately.”
Read the full report here.
Issues within the department have been simmering for years after anonymous employees’ complaints to Metro councilmembers.
In November, a current DEC employee publicly alleged that her harassment complaints had not been adequately addressed, triggering the outside review.

The investigator found that employees “consistently reported that Director Martini’s management practices and management style have also created a pervasive culture of fear, dissatisfaction and disengagement at DEC.”
Some of those interviewed provided information about Martini’s leadership only on the condition that it not be specifically included in the final report, out of fear of punishment, the report notes.

“It is unfortunate that it took eight months of work on behalf of the Women’s Caucus for the mayor’s office to realize the staff was telling the truth all along,” Metro Councilmember Joy Styles, who spearheaded a months-long pressure campaign against Martini and solicited current and former employee feedback, told the Banner .
“Had they just taken the time to talk to staff and not gaslit people, we could have saved the staff months of additional heartache.”
Unlike some director-level positions in Metro, Martini’s role is subject to civil service rules.
Patrice Coleman, a deputy in the department, will serve as interim director while the civil service disciplinary process unfolds.

“We are grateful that this administration has put the safety of Nashville citizens and visitors at the forefront of this issue,” said Maura Lee Albert of SEIU, which represents workers in the department.

“Employees at DEC have bravely been speaking out for years about their working conditions, and we appreciate their courageous actions that have helped bring about the changes needed to make DEC a safe and productive workplace.”

Steve Martini — Metro Nashville’s director of emergency communications, who was placed on leave last month — has been fired.
Alex Apple, a spokesperson with the mayor's office, confirmed Martini’s termination — effective Feb.
2 — with Scene sister publication the Nashville Post .
Martini initially rejected Mayor Freddie O’Connell’s request for a resignation and instead was placed on administrative leave in January.
This followed an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment, intimidation and mismanagement, all spanning multiple years.
Emergency Communications Director Placed on Leave
Investigation outlines ‘pervasive culture of fear, dissatisfaction and disengagement’ under Stephen Martini
Law firm Ogletree Deakins sent a 13-page report to Metro legal director Wally Dietz on Jan.
9 outlining a “pervasive culture of fear, dissatisfaction and disengagement” created by Martini.

The report found that complaints made to the Department of Emergency Communications' human resources department were not investigated or handled properly and that many employees of the department did not come forward to with specific details regarding the allegations due to fear of retaliation.

“The majority of interviewees indicated that employees have consistently reported feeling intimidated by Director Martini’s leadership style and certain leadership practices/decisions, which have fostered an atmosphere of anxiety and distrust,” the report reads.
The Metro Council unanimously passed a resolution in December pushing for the mayor’s office and DEC to enact change over the department’s leadership and workplace culture.
Since Martini was placed on administrative leave, Patrice Coleman has served as interim director of the department.
She is the current deputy director of operations.

Another $1.5M without accounting for the last $4.4M | What happens when homelessness is managed like a product line & funded like a slush fund
Nashville handed homelessness to a well connected executive who oversaw the merger of stolen foreign data grown into a $22.1m ICE contract.

Mar 03, 2026
I received feedback yesterday that my previous post was too harsh on the nonprofits keeping the lights on in this city.
That criticism is not unwarranted.

In highlighting the gap between eviction prevention funding and outcomes, I was equating the actions of Metro Nashville with the organizations working exhaustive hours on razor-thin margins to fill gaps that government is designed to fill.
That isn’t fair, and it isn’t accurate.

A specific correction from yesterday’s post: the organization requesting emails from those in urgent need of rental assistance was a “downstream” funding provider, not The United Way — and I’m told feedback is being given about the barriers this may present.
Also, while many volunteers did fill in gaps during the crisis, it was an overstatement to say there was an “army” waiting to help out.
Please reach out and support the orgs I mentioned , but let’s do all ask ourselves the hard questions about how we can aim our support at helping those most likely to be evicted.
Which brings us back to OHS…

Let’s turn our attention to those who are creating the very gaps that are meant to be filled by the government — and see what it looks like when a city operates its most vulnerable systems like a business, offloads its duties to nonprofits it uses as an auxiliary backup government, and then wonders why it isn’t working for anyone except the those driving the evictions.
This latest proposed allocation to OHS is a chapter in a history book that is being written — figuratively, for now.

It is a book about how the mayor’s office, acting through the Office of Homeless Services, spent $50 million in federal recovery funds dedicated to homelessness, who benefited, and who looked the other way.

The contracts, the invoices, the late files, the sole-source arrangements, the threshold structuring, the landlords paid for rooms whether they’re filled or not — all of it is being documented, sourced, and connected in real time.
Everyone who touches this system becomes a character.
The people who built it.
The people who benefited from it.
And the people who had the authority to ask questions and chose not to.
Tonight, Metro Council will vote on a late-filed resolution adding $1.5 million to a contract with the Hospitality Hub of Memphis to operate interim housing at the Rodeway Inn on Wallace Road.

This brings the total contract to nearly $4 million — for a Memphis nonprofit with no Nashville track record, paying $1.54 million in rent to RIA, LLC , the entity controlled by Rodeway owner Shabana Ali, for a property she purchased for $667,500 in 2010 and that the city now appraises at $3.1 million .
RS2025-1711: The prior resolution that requests a spending plan from OHS for keeping people housed, which has not been supplied.
There is no transition plan, no tenant protections, and no answers to the questions Council already asked about the last $4.4m check they cut for OHS they’re supposed to provide a spending plan for.
This latest allocations was signed by four Metro officials over 10 days ago but dropped on Council as a late file.
The question nobody has answered: why?

Why the Missing Spending Plan Matters Right Now

The reason Council’s unanimously requested spending plan matters — the reason it matters tonight — is that Nashville’s eviction crisis is accelerating and the system the mayor’s office built to address it is failing on both ends simultaneously.
As {Rich Text} reported yesterday, funding that was supposed to keep people from being evicted and flowing into homelessness is not showing up for those who need it most.

And today, breaking news from eviction court: Jennifer McCoy’s firm, the single highest-volume eviction attorney in Nashville, representing approximately one-third of all eviction filings, is not accepting any money on behalf of her tenants and is refusing to participate in diversion court at all.

From someone on-site on March 3 2026: Jennifer McCoy's firm refuses to accept rental assistance payments and will not provide tenants with their outstanding balances, which would allow them to seek funding independently.
Of the more than 200 cases on today's docket, only two individuals were deemed eligible for storm relief, despite over a hundred defendants meeting the eligibility criteria.
This effectively renders the city’s efforts to slow the increase in homelessness null.
One attorney’s non-participation neutralizes the entire diversion infrastructure for a third of the caseload.

So what Council is looking at is a system where money flows freely to places like the Rodeway Inn and to landlords housing people in volatile, undocumented conditions — and is rewarded for it — while the front end of the pipeline, where people lose their housing in the first place, goes unfunded and unanswered.
The $4.4 million spending plan Council unanimously requested under RS2025-1711 was supposed to address exactly this: how does the city prevent Nashvillians from losing their permanent housing?
The mayor’s office has refused to answer.
Tonight they want $1.5 million more for the back end.
And the money that has been spent is not confined to formal contracts.
OHS has made over $350,000 in rent payments directly to various landlords outside of any procurement process or contract authorization.
Please sit with this previously unreported fact.
I made a database to explore this shocking phenomenon.
It all has to do with “business unit 53902028,” funding that was supposed to go to Strobel House (and then some of it was legimitately reallocated for a few ‘competitive grants’).
What you can see plainly is that much of this money went to “rent” payments to landlords that had precisely ZERO contract with Metro authorizing them to receive funding in this volume.
I’ve made sure those running the ongoing internal audit were aware of this and have also noticed local media.
https://clovenbradshaw-ctrl.github.io/53902028/
OHS has has made it clear to many that they “do not pay rent”.
Invoices like the above say otherwise.

It speaks to an illicit, off-the-books system where the priority is to remove people from politically undesirable places and stick them somewhere by any means necessary, procurement and housing first best practices be damned.
Yet many people I’ve spoken to say that, dating back to January 2024, this is what happened to them:
• They are placed into a facility by the city with promised for a year of support and a housing voucher.
• They are led to sign leases.
They are not given a copy of those leases, or any documentation of this arrangement of support from OHS.
• And then the support stops, sometimes with the tenants learning that Metro has not been paying their rent for months.

• With Metro appearing no where on their leases, it is the tenants, people who had previously been living in encampments in the throes of addiction, who end up in eviction court with judgements against them.
This is pattern happening at a scale that I am still trying to get a hold of, but it is not a “few times” thing.
Two families have now filed formal Title VI Civil Rights complaints against OHS and Metro for these actions.

Take Wallace Studios at 97 Wallace Road — a separate property down the street from the Rodeway — it received nearly $100,000 in unauthorized furniture purchases and tens of thousands of dollars in direct rent payments, all outside any contract that would authorize the expenditure.
These are not appropriated funds flowing through approved channels.
They are discretionary payments made by OHS to landlords with no competitive bidding, no Council oversight, and no documented obligations to the tenants those payments were supposed to protect.

And this is precisely what the $4M that Metro Council wants a spending plan on seems geared to do, with Director Calvin’s language explaining how it will be “made available to Metro Officials” reading like a (speaking figuratively) bribe to have them look the other way.

What’s clear to me is the the money Council is asking an accounting for is just a slightly more legitimate version of how they’ve been spending money for years, with these off-the-books rent payments with money not allocated for that and no contract validating it dating back to 2024.
The Business Approach to Homelessness
When Kristin Wilson was hired by the City of Atlanta, the press release said the quiet part out loud.
Her “strong corporate background” would be an asset as the city sought to “improve business functions and efficiency” and “make real progress on the issue of street homelessness.”
The City of Atlanta did not explain why her professional background in corporate America gave her any sort of insight on “street homelessness.”

Here’s the full passage:
Ms.
Wilson’s experience managing multi-million dollar acquisitions and strategic projects make her an ideal candidate to lead the City of Atlanta’s new Innovation Delivery Team,” Mayor Reed said.
“Her strong corporate background will be an asset to the city as we seek to improve business functions and efficiency across the city and make real progress on the issue of street homelessness.
Wilson had managed $50 million in revenue at LexisNexis and coordinated the overall integration of the $4.1 billion acquisition of ChoicePoint by LexisNexis .
What Wilson integrated was not an ordinary data company.
ChoicePoint had purchased Mexico’s entire voter registration database for $250,000 and sold it to the U.S.
government through a contract with the Immigration and Naturalization Service — data that is strictly confidential under Mexican law .
The Mexican Federal Electoral Institute filed criminal complaints and one of the people responsible “went into hiding”.

Before that, ChoicePoint had acquired the employee screening business of Pinkerton’s — America’s first private detective agency , founded in 1849, notorious for strikebreaking and labor infiltration — including a proprietary database called Esteem, which tracked retail employees who had admitted to workplace theft .
A subsequent lawsuit let to LexisNexis settling millions for laborers who were discriminated against despite being charged for no crimes.
ChoicePoint’s contracts with the INS helped lay the groundwork for LexisNexis’ current $22.1 million contract with ICE to provide information on the location of over 276 million Americans .
Wilson coordinated the integration of all of it — Pinkerton’s surveillance tools, stolen foreign voter data, and a global data brokerage infrastructure — into a single platform.
Then she was brought into government to run homelessness the way you’d run a product line.
Wilson is now Nashville’s Chief of Operations and Performance.
As the Nashville Scene reported , Mayor Cooper, knowing there was heat on Nashville from the state comptroller, named Kristin Wilson chief of operations immediately upon taking office.
Her husband, the Nashville scene reported, is the son of Justin P. Wilson , Tennessee’s Comptroller of the Treasury until 2021 — the office responsible for fiscal oversight of local government.
The city has seemingly operated with autonomy from the Comptroller’s office.

The system the mayor’s office, acting through OHS, oversees here — sole-source contracts, consultants cycling between advisory roles and paid engagements, nonprofits awarded millions with no local track record, landlords paid whether rooms are filled or not — is what a market approach to homelessness looks like.

That system was made possible in part by a structural change: when Council created the Office of Homeless Services, then–Council Member Freddie O’Connell amended the legislation on the floor to make OHS report directly to the mayor’s office rather than through normal Board or Commission oversight.

The effect, after subsequent retooling of our homelessness system, was to place Nashville’s entire homelessness apparatus — its Continuum of Care, its Coordinated Entry system, its HMIS data, its vendor relationships — under direct mayoral control, with Kristin Wilson’s office as the point of coordination.
Its target audience was always the business class: clean the encampments, move the numbers, signal progress.
The question this article asks is what that approach looks like for the people it claims to serve.
People I’ve spoken with who were placed at the Rodeway from the Hermitage encampment describe conditions that should trouble anyone voting to extend this operation.
They are now homeless again.
Their full accounts are forthcoming.
What It Was Like Inside
{Rich Text} has spoken with eight people who were taken from the Hermitage encampment and placed at the Rodeway Inn during the Salvation Army’s operation of the facility.
All eight are now experiencing homelessness again.

Their accounts — which will be reported in full in a forthcoming piece — describe a facility whose operating structure was designed by April Calvin while she was still at the Salvation Army, before she was appointed OHS Director.
According to those that were housed there, residents were discouraged by staff from seeking employment on the theory that earned income would jeopardize pending benefits applications.
In many cases, those benefits never materialized.
The result was a population with no legal income, no meaningful case management, and no clear path to permanent housing.
One former resident alleges that without the ability to earn legitimate income, she and others turned to sex work to survive.
Residents describe being warehoused, not housed — placed in rooms and left to wait for a system that never showed up for them.
When the placements fell apart, there was no safety net.
No transition plan.
No follow-up.
They went back to the street.
These conditions existed under the previous operator, one that Director Calvin had worked at in a role central to these operations for over 20 years prior to joining Metro.

Council is now being asked to nearly double the funding for the current operator — at a facility with the same owner, the same oversight from the mayor’s office, and the same contract structure — without any evidence that what happens inside those rooms has changed.
And if the follow the same rubber stamping indifference to performing actual oversight, they’ll likely give it to them.
Character choices in the history book of Nashville.
Council Is Owed an Answer It Hasn’t Gotten

In December, Council unanimously passed RS2025-1711 non-bindingly asking the Office of Homeless Services to present a plan for how it would use its $4.4 million budget increase to prevent Nashvillians from losing their permanent housing.
The mayor’s office fought that resolution.
It passed anyway.
OHS has not delivered the plan.
It’s been more than two months.

At the last Homelessness Planning Council meeting, OHS Assistant Director of Planning and Research Allison Cantway said providing a plan “was not the intent” of a resolution whose title literally says “allocate funding to ensure no Nashvillians lose their permanent housing.”
So the mayor’s office, acting through OHS, is asking for $1.5 million more tonight while actively refusing to account for the $4.4 million Council already gave them.
The Budget Lines Deserve Questions
The revised budget in this amendment raises questions that deserve time and scrutiny.

The occupancy line on the grant sits at $1.54 million — rent to RIA, LLC , the entity controlled by Rodeway owner Shabana Ali, for a property appraised at $3.1 million that she purchased for $667,500 — and whose owner once offered rooms to the city for free.
Security is $833,000 for a roughly 90-room motel.
Travel and conferences is $118,000 — for an interim housing operation.
And there is zero recipient match across every single line item.
These aren’t gotcha questions.
They’re the kind of questions the normal legislative process exists to surface.
So why the late file?
We don’t know.
But the pattern is familiar.

Since Kristin Wilson arrived in Nashville, the homelessness system has operated on a consistent principle: move fast, keep it vague, and structure things so that by the time anyone with oversight authority gets a look, the money is already out the door.
How This Contract Came to Exist
The Rodeway Inn was previously managed by the Salvation Army under a gap housing contract that ran through October 2024.

According to sources intimately familiar with the arrangement, that contract was written intentionally vague — consistent with what multiple recipients of major OHS contracts describe as a preference, originating from the mayor’s office, for language loose enough that funds can be moved without clear tracking.

When the Salvation Army’s new operators grew frustrated with demands from OHS that went beyond anything the contract actually required, they pointed out that the agreement contained no terms of service obligating them to comply — and rescinded their collaboration.
OHS Assistant Director Cantway then publicly accused the Salvation Army of refusing to use a separate $1.9 million grant for gap housing.
NewsChannel 5 reviewed the documents and confirmed the Salvation Army was right: the grant was written for their LIFNAV outreach program, not Rodeway operations.
This is the pattern.
Contracts are written without clear obligations.
When partners push back, they are blamed publicly.
And the lack of specificity is not a bug — it is the operating method, and it has been since Wilson’s office took the reins.

It is the same method behind the mayor’s office’s refusal to deliver the $4.4 million spending plan Council unanimously requested under RS2025-1711 — a resolution that faced direct opposition from Kristin Wilson’s office before it passed anyway.
And it is the same method behind tonight’s late file: present the spending as urgent, compress the timeline, and trust that Council won’t say no to money that’s supposed to help homeless people.
Meanwhile, motel owner Ali had 80 rooms ready since March 2024 and told reporters she was “kept in the dark.”
FOX 17 reported that only 30 of the Rodeway’s 110 beds were occupied.
Council members expressed alarm.
Nothing happened.
Within two months of the Salvation Army’s departure, a Memphis-based nonprofit with zero Nashville track record received a contract for nearly $2.5 million for the site.
That contract is now being expanded to nearly $4 million — tonight, as a late file.
The Precedent: How the Mayor’s Office Built This System
This pattern has a longer history, and it traces directly to the mayor’s office, acting through OHS — not to any single department acting alone.
In 2022, the Cooper administration brought in Stacy Horn Koch — operating through Housing NOLA, a New Orleans-based entity — to produce a homelessness study.
The contract was sole-source and cost $500,000.
Open Table Nashville’s Paula Foster called the result “a colossal waste of $500,000, to tell us exactly what we already knew.”
A comparable assessment by Focus Strategies in 2015 had cost $25,000.
But what Ms.

Foster likely could net yet see is that is this was not a simple report being drafted, it was the first salvo of war to redesign the entire homelessness system around Nashville’s highest executive, and more specifically, reporting directly to Kristin Wilson.
Koch had a prior working relationship with Kristin Wilson.
In Atlanta, Wilson served as Deputy Chief Operating Officer while Koch served as Interim Director of Human Services.
Wilson’s office was Koch’s largest single source of payments from the City of Atlanta.
When Wilson came to Nashville as Cooper’s Chief of Operations and Performance, Koch’s contract followed.

Six months after Koch presented her study, her entity received a second contract — this one for “Assistance with homeless encampment closures,” sole-source, designated high-risk, with no Council legislation required.
The initial amount was $237,100.
It was then amended by exactly $12,900 — bringing the total to exactly $250,000, the threshold at which Metro Code requires Council approval.
In other words: the contract was structured in two installments that kept the total just below the line where Council would have had to vote on it.
This is the same pattern as tonight’s late file — not identical in mechanism, but identical in function.
The money moves before oversight can engage.

As recently as December 2024, the Outdoor Homelessness Strategy approved by the Homelessness Planning Council still describes Koch as a “mayoral advisor” who helped develop the original encampment strategy — language that frames what was supposed to be a one-time consulting engagement as an ongoing advisory relationship with no visible end date.
The original Nashville contract for Koch had a single Council sponsor: then–District 19 Council Member Freddie O’Connell.
The Eviction Pipeline
Council members are increasingly being evaluated by the number of evictions in their districts.

Every time the mayor’s office, acting through OHS, places someone in housing without a master lease, without documented tenant rights, without copies of their own lease agreements, and that placement falls apart — an eviction gets filed.
It shows up in the data.
It reflects on the district and its Council Member.
The track record is already clear at Wallace Studios.
Eviction filing after eviction filing — including against people OHS placed there using “landlord engagement funds” with no underlying contract.
Families were promised vouchers that never came, or that were processed so slowly landlords initiated eviction before the paperwork cleared.
Tonight’s $1.5 million creates the same exposure at 95 Wallace.
The Hospitality Hub contract pays for occupancy whether rooms are filled or not.
But there is no documented transition plan for what happens to residents when the contract ends in June 2026.
There is no master lease protecting them.
There is no evidence their rights are documented.
Council is being asked to fund the front end of a housing pipeline whose back end is eviction court.
The ARPA Clock Is the Excuse, Not the Reason
All of this money flows from ARPA funds originally allocated to Shared Equity Housing under RS2022-1860 , then reallocated to homeless services under RS2024-490 .
It must be spent by December 31, 2026, or returned to the federal government.
That creates pressure to approve spending fast and ask questions later.
But the ARPA deadline is not a surprise.
The mayor’s office, acting through OHS, has known about it for years.
There are nine months of runway.
So what makes this a late file?
What changed between last week and tonight that required bypassing the normal filing timeline?
Nobody has said.
But the answer may be simpler than it looks: this is how the system has operated since Kristin Wilson’s office took control of homelessness spending.
The Koch contract was structured to avoid Council approval.
The Salvation Army contract was written vague enough to avoid enforceable obligations.
The $350,000 in landlord payments went out without procurement.
Tonight’s late file is not an aberration.
It is the method.
Who This Administration Works For

Two weeks ago, Tom Morales — the man who saved the Loveless Cafe, the Woolworth building, and Acme Feed and Seed — told the mayor his property taxes had gone from $129,000 to $600,000 in a single year and asked for a meeting .
The mayor wouldn’t take it.
When FOX 17 asked O’Connell directly, his response included the line: “It’s not up to me whether he keeps that business open.
The market evolves.
New businesses start even as beloved old businesses close.”
His office later accused FOX 17 of selective editing, but the station published the unedited version and stood by its reporting.
Council Member Kupin, who represents downtown, said he was “appalled” .
That’s the market, baby.
But if you’re a landlord housing people off the books, using funding not legally set aside for these purposes, expect this administration to send good money after bad.
The Rodeway’s owner paid $667,500 for the property in 2010 .
Now she’s collecting $1.54 million in “occupancy” from a single contract period — more than twice what she paid for the entire building.
Wallace Studios collected hundreds of thousands in unauthorized rent, furniture, and landlord engagement payments — and evicted a quarter of its tenants, including people OHS placed there.

Tonight, Council is being asked to approve nearly $4 million total for a Memphis nonprofit with no Nashville track record to continue operating a facility with no transition plan, no tenant protections, and no answers to the questions Council already asked — all as a late file, with no explanation for the urgency.
Acme Feed and Seed can’t get a meeting.
These landlords can’t stop getting checks.
Mr.

Morales might consider renting out space in his building for the unhoused and operating it like (as former residents have described the Rodeway Inn “an indoor encampment, but worse because you can’t choose who your neighbors are”).
Maybe then he could get time on Ms.
Wilson’s calendar.

Liberal Bullshittery: An Autopsy of a Democracy
What a Nashville budget hearing reveals about how progressive cities build the infrastructure for authoritarian capture — one sole-source contract at a time.

Rich Text
May 13, 2026
“Explain it to me as if I was a 5th grader, how the expenditures per capita have nearly tripled — and what measurable outcomes she could point to.”
— Councilwoman Ellis, Metro Council Public Health and Safety Committee, May 7, 2026
I’d like to tell you about a budget meeting that happened a few days ago — one of over 50 that our Metro Council members must unfortunately suffer through each spring.
All of these departmental budgets have previously been passed through the desk of the Mayor’s Director of Operations and Performance, Kristin Wilson.

You may remember her from previous reporting : she is the mayor’s office official who coordinated Nashville’s $15 million surveillance agreement with the Downtown Partnership, and who, before entering government, helped build the data infrastructure that ICE now uses to track immigrants.
Put a pin in that name.

I want to discuss this particular hearing because it is a case study in what I’ll call — with what sounds like glib derision at first, but I actually mean in a very precise sense — liberal bullshittery .

To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
This is a story about homelessness.
But it is not only a story about homelessness.

It is about how democratic governance gets converted into ungovernable corporate governance under progressive branding — and how that conversion, happening quietly in city budget hearings across the country, is the precondition for the authoritarian capture we are watching unfold at the national level.
A budget hearing for a two-year-old department in a mid-size Southern city is a strange place to see this clearly.

But it is the right place, because this is where it actually happens: not in manifestos or think tanks, but in line items, sole-source contracts, and the systematic removal of every mechanism that would let the public know what is being done in its name.
Here's the thing: scrutinizing the funding of a homelessness department is not gotcha politics.
It is not about scoring points or embarrassing an administration.
It is about the fact that unhoused people are, by every empirical measure, the most vulnerable population in our society.

They are the most likely to be sexually assaulted, the most likely to be sex trafficked, the most likely to have their very bodies collected, dissected, and sold for profit without their consent or their families' knowledge.

When we allow the agencies charged with serving this population to operate without clear, rigorous oversight, when we tolerate opaque budgets, unreviewed contracts, and a culture of institutional secrecy around how public dollars are spent, we are not merely risking inefficiency or waste.
We are, unequivocally, increasing the amount of violent harm that human beings will suffer.
The misuse of public funds is never acceptable.
The lack of candor about their deployment is never acceptable.

But directing that misuse and that secrecy toward the most powerless people in our city, people who cannot lobby, cannot litigate, cannot call a press conference, and whose disappearance from public life is treated not as an emergency but as an aesthetic improvement, is unconscionable.
Oversight is not an attack.
It is the bare minimum of what a democratic society owes to those it has already failed.
And to fight that oversight is to take the side of the sex traffickers, illegal corpse resellers, and extortionists who see our unhoused neighbors not as humans but as easy prey.
But back to “Liberal Bullshittery.”

By liberal , I mean it in the sense of neoliberalism: a system that views government as a means to open up the marketplace for profit, and that government services exist to the extent they help the wealthy extract value from places of commerce.
And by bullshit , I mean it precisely as the philosopher Harry Frankfurt defined it : speech unconcerned with whether it is true or false, only with whether it is persuasive.
The bullshitter is not a liar.
The liar knows the truth and says the opposite.

The bullshitter is worse: unmoored from the question of truth entirely, speaking fluently about data and best practices, right some of the time, but fundamentally unconcerned with whether what she is describing is actually working — because the system she operates in is not designed to answer that question.
It is designed to avoid it.

Here is the state of play: Nashville’s homeless services network has been systematically redesigned by a former data-broker executive who was parachuted into city government, funded by a billionaire’s philanthropy, to apply corporate strategy to a complex human services ecosystem she had no experience in.

That system now imports consulting models built for downtown business districts, spends public money outside procurement law, and has castrated the one local governing body that could hold it accountable.
The people closest to the problem, outreach workers, case managers, the unhoused themselves, are the last to be consulted and the first to be overridden.

The political economist Elinor Ostrom spent a career proving that this is precisely how you destroy a commons: not through neglect, but through confident outside intervention that dismantles the local institutional knowledge and trust networks communities spent decades building.

Curtis Yarvin, a Silicon Valley software engineer turned blogger, bankrolled by Peter Thiel, and godfather of the anti-democratic “Dark Enlightenment” movement, has a name for what this looks like when it is done on purpose.
He calls it neocameralism: the state run as a corporation, the executive as CEO-monarch, democratic oversight dissolved as inefficiency.
In his writings, Yarvin sorts humanity into racial categories he calls “elves, hobbits, dwarves, orcs, and zombies.”
His operational plan, which he calls RAGE (Retire All Government Employees), is widely recognized as the blueprint for Musk’s DOGE.
Vice President Vance cited Yarvin by name and said Trump should “fire every single mid-level bureaucrat” and ignore the courts when they push back.
Yarvin attended Trump’s inaugural ball.
But a government cannot just become a corporation over night.
The people who redesigned Nashville’s homeless services system have almost certainly never read, or likely have even heard of Curtis Yarvin.
Yet they are building precisely what he describes, doing it in the name of “innovation” and “efficiency.”
You will recognize this pattern by the end of this piece.
But first, how would we actually end homelessness, if that was a thing we actually wanted to do?
Sam Tsemberis proved it in 1992 : give people permanent housing without preconditions, with support services available but not required, and 85–90% stay housed .
Finland proved it nationally .
The VA proved it with veterans.

Will Connelly, who ran both Nashville’s Homelessness Commission and Metro Denver’s Homeless Initiative , put the test simply: “A real system is defined by whether those efforts are aligned around a single, measurable goal: helping people exit homelessness quickly and permanently.”
We do not have a system that sets a clear goal like this that honestly appraises it's progress.
But even its leaders know what the resource problem really is, if they come up empty handed for any real ideas to solve it.
Office of Homeless Services Director April Calvin told the Metro Council committee on Wednesday that “housing is what we need more of.”
It is not her office’s remit to develop decomodified housing.
What is it that they do instead?
She described her office as “data-driven.”
She claims that it is an in-joke in her office that she asks, before making any decision, “Show me the data.”
And then she presented a budget that revealed a system designed to avoid being held accountable to any of it.
The question that couldn’t be answered simply
Nashville has spent $50 million in federal ARPA funds on homelessness since October 2022.
OHS’s budget has grown to FY27 ask of $10,318,000 from the general budget.
The results: housing placements are down 13% year over year.
The 2025 PIT count , revealed on a single budget slide Wednesday, shows 2,180 people, a 4.1% increase.
For every one person Nashville houses, 2.5 enter homelessness.
Councilwoman Tasha Ellis asked about the per-capita spending.
She wanted something she could explain to constituents, specifically to a group of kids at her bus stop who pay attention to this issue.

Calvin’s response was that OHS had shifted from housing “the easy to house” to addressing “chronic-level homelessness,” meaning people with longer histories of living outside, more complex needs, higher costs.
When you serve harder cases, she said, “you’re going to have to pay a little bit longer.”
That makes intuitive sense.
Harder cases cost more per person.
But Calvin had already explained, earlier in the same hearing, how her budget was organized, and the explanation contradicts the answer she gave Ellis.
Nashville’s homeless services system has two funding tracks.
The first is coordinated entry , the federal system that uses a scored vulnerability assessment to prioritize who gets housed.
Calvin described it clearly: coordinated entry “is focused on the most vulnerable individuals,” people with co-occurring disorders, long lengths of time outside, the highest needs.
This is the chronic population.
It already has a pipeline.
The second track is what Calvin calls MRRF , Metro Rapid Response Funds.
This is new local money, created last budget cycle.
Calvin described it as being for people who “may not ever really need to wait for that level of trauma to — so that they can get a higher score to be funded through the coordinated entry process.”
In other words: MRRF is explicitly for people who are not the most vulnerable.
It exists because coordinated entry only reaches the hardest cases, and Calvin wanted flexible dollars for everyone else.
So: coordinated entry already serves the chronic, hardest-to-house population.
MRRF was designed for people outside that population.
But when Ellis asked why outcomes are declining despite more spending, Calvin’s answer was that they’re now serving the chronic, hardest-to-house population — and that’s why it costs more.
Both justifications cannot be true about the same system at the same time.

If coordinated entry, the system long in place before Calvin joined Metro, already serves the most vulnerable, and MRRF was built for everyone else, then declining outcomes can’t be explained by saying you’re doing harder work — because the harder work was already happening through the other track.
The question is: what the new money is doing, for whom, and why the numbers are moving in the wrong direction.
That question went unanswered.
The appearance of circumventing
Later in the hearing, Calvin said something that helps explain what MRRF is actually for.

At 56:34, describing why she wants additional funding beyond coordinated entry, Calvin told the committee:
“Thinking of our coordinated entry process and how some of those individuals have been on the list for a very long time, may not have the high score to be housed by way of the coordinated entry process.
We’re looking for additional funds where we would not have to appear to circumvent a system or put someone in front of.”
Check the tape on that one.
The director is not saying MRRF prevents circumvention of the federal priority system.
She is saying she wants money so that when her office houses someone outside the priority list, it doesn’t look like they’re circumventing it.
The concern is not the bypass.
It is the appearance.
And appearance is, with all Liberal Bullshittery, all that matters.
Let's be clear: MRRF has no published scoring criteria.
It has no public prioritization list.
No external body reviews how the funds are distributed.

When Councilwoman Evans asked whether MRRF has an end date — “when we use pilot, it implies it’s going to end at some point” — Calvin said “October 2026,” at which point they’d “look at the data, review the data, and then figure out the next steps.”
A pilot without success criteria and an end date that falls after the budget cycle is not a pilot.
It is a permanent discretionary fund used however she, but more to the point, the Mayor’s Office, wants to use it.
When Calvin first introduced MRRF to the Homelessness Planning Council in November 2025, she described the funds as being “made available to Metro Officials.”
Not to case managers.
Not to people on the by-name list.
To officials.
The framing tells you who the intended user is.
And the name itself is new.
“MRRF” did not exist as a program until November 2025.
Before that, the same money appeared in the Metro budget as “Non-Traditional Rapid Re-Housing.”
That term is not a term of art in any federal, state, or evidence-based homeless services model.
It returns exactly one search result: a FOX 17 article quoting Calvin.

She invented a program name, put it in a budget document, got it funded, renamed it to MRRF after reporting revealed the unauthorized placements and evictions it had already produced, and is now asking for it to be expanded.
In the FY27 budget modifications the committee reviewed Wednesday, MRRF does not appear as its own line item at all.
It has been folded into “Community Case Management Funding,” a $2 million ask whose justification text mentions that it “will compliment last year’s MRRF and PSH funding.”
Three names in three budget cycles for the same discretionary money with no published criteria.
Each rename makes it harder to track.
Renaming something euphemistically, or renaming it out of view entirely: there perhaps is no better manifestation of liberal bullshittery.
I haven’t read this yet.
Seems like a good time.
The number that sounds too good
OHS has cited an 85% retention rate for people it places in housing, meaning only 15% return to homelessness.

If true, this would be an extraordinary outcome — matching the results Tsemberis achieved with Pathways Housing First under controlled conditions with permanent supportive housing and voluntary wraparound services.
I am calling bullshit on this number.
An 85% retention rate would require actively verifying that the people placed in housing are still there.

After talking to former OHS employees, to case managers in the field, and to people who were placed by OHS and subsequently evicted or otherwise lost their housing, I have found no evidence that OHS is conducting any such verification.
Literally, it seems that no one proactively checks to see if people are still housed.

From what I can determine, the 15% displacement rate represents only those individuals who re-entered the homeless services system and were successfully re-identified in HMIS — not duplicated as a new record, but matched to their existing case.
A former staffer on the landlord engagement team confirmed that duplicate records are common and that no, they do not actively check to ensure people have not been displaced.
This means the 85% figure does not measure how many people are still housed.
It measures how many people who lost their housing managed to find their way back into the system and were correctly re-entered.
This is survivorship bias : counting only the cases that remain visible to the system and treating everyone who disappears as a success.
The audit no one mentioned
Councilwoman Zulfat Suara went directly at the landlord program: “I’ve had complaints about slum landlords and people being evicted and a revolving door for people that we’re putting in homes.”

Calvin deflected, suggesting the revolving door might be a service provider’s problem, then described plans to fix it — all things that should already exist in a program that has spent over $350,000 in rent payments outside any procurement contract.
Councilwoman Evans followed up with a case from her own district: “a landlord ended up evicting somebody, potentially more than one person, just because they had the right to do it.”
OHS didn’t have the capacity to intervene.
What Suara and Evans were describing, from opposite ends of the same problem, are the programs currently under investigation.
Calvin did talk about the importance of oversight in the meeting, but not of her department, but by her department over others.
She told the committee she wanted “accountability, transparency, and performance-based” practices over the community organizations they provide money to.
OHS is not well positioned to be overseeing financial practices of anyone.

What she did not mention, and no committee member raised, is that OHS is currently under a formal Metro audit requested by Councilmember Ginny Welsch and approved by the Audit Committee in September 2025.
The audit request cites $3.2 million in potential financial irregularities.
The Office of Internal Audit was already separately investigating $500,000 in “landlord engagement” spending.
The programs Calvin was citing as successes are the programs under investigation.

Nashville Scene reporting found that Calvin hand-picked families from the Nashville Rescue Mission and moved them to private landlords on verbal rent guarantees, no contract, no competitive bidding, no documented obligations to the tenants.
Rent payments came late or not at all.
In at least two cases, landlords initiated eviction proceedings against the people OHS was supposed to be housing.
OHS has made over $350,000 in direct rent payments to landlords outside any procurement process.

I have been provided multiple email chains showing people placed in housing through MRRF or similar areangements facing eviction while OHS was non-responsive, and at least one case where OHS attempted to shift responsibility to a third-party case manager who believed she was being set up to take the fall for a displacement that OHS’s own off-contract placement process created.

DePaul USA, the operator of Strobel House (which Calvin described to the committee as under OHS “oversight”), billed over $1 million against a $500,000 contract, submitting retroactive invoices for a service period the contract had already covered.
Calvin acknowledged the overrun in a July 2024 email to councilmembers.
Four incidents at Strobel (two fires, a stabbing, and an employee injury) reportedly occurred during a period when Metro did not have an active contract with DePaul.
The only apparent accountability to date: DePaul’s CEO, after 15 years in the position, departed after these revelations surfaced.
Mayor O’Connell’s office has taken no public acts of oversight since the audit was approved in September.
In December, Metro Council unanimously passed RS2025-1711 , asking OHS to present a plan for how it would use its $4.4 million budget increase.
OHS and the mayor’s office opposed the resolution.
It passed anyway.

OHS eventually did deliver a response, but it did not resemble what was requested: no methodology for who would receive funds, no prioritization criteria, no framework that would distinguish MRRF from a slush fund used to move unhoused people at the direction of council members and department heads.
Calvin opened the hearing on Wednesday by describing OHS as “a 2-year-old department” eager to share “the great strides that we’ve made with, and some of the challenges that we had along the way.”

Payments outside contracts, invoices exceeding authorizations, families moved on verbal guarantees and then evicted, a CEO resignation, and a Council-mandated spending plan answered with a non-answer: these are not challenges along the way.
They are a pattern.
And Calvin did not design it.
Remember that pin?
The Designer of Operations
Kristin Wilson, the Mayor’s Director of Operations and Performance, meets with every department to help shape the budget the mayor requests from Council.
She is also the person who built Nashville’s homeless services system.
Before Nashville, Wilson was placed in Atlanta city government by Bloomberg Philanthropies , which invested $3.3 million to create an Innovation Delivery Team under Mayor Kasim Reed.
Her mandate: improve relationships with the business community and and reduce street homelessness.
In that order.
Before Atlanta, Wilson was Vice President of Market Planning at LexisNexis Risk Solutions, where she managed $50 million in revenue.
A data-broker executive, funded by a billionaire’s philanthropy, installed in city government to apply corporate strategy to the management of homeless bodies in commercial corridors.
Wilson came to Nashville on Cooper’s first day in office as his Chief of Operations and Performance.

Nashville Scene reported that she was hired in the context of pressure from the state comptroller’s office on the city’s finances; her father-in-law was Justin Wilson , Tennessee’s long-time state comptroller , now comptroller emeritus.
Two years later, the Cooper administration commissioned Stacy Horn Koch — who had worked alongside Wilson in Atlanta — to conduct a $500,000 study of Nashville’s homeless services.
Then-Councilmember Freddie O’Connell sponsored the legislation.
The study’s entity was Housing NOLA, a Louisiana nonprofit.
Open Table Nashville’s executive director called it “a colossal waste of $500,000, to tell us exactly what we already knew.”
A comparable assessment by Focus Strategies in 2015 reached substantially similar conclusions for $25,000.
Koch’s study produced the framework for the current system.

Then Koch received a second contract through Housing NOLA to implement her own recommendations — a well-documented ethical problem in which the person diagnosing the problem is also the one paid to fix it.
That second contract: “assistance with homeless encampment closures,” was initially set at $237,100, exactly $12,900 under the $250,000 threshold requiring Metro Council approval.
It was then amended to $250,000, designated IDIQ (Indefinite Delivery/Indefinite Quantity), sole source, and flagged “High Risk” by the Finance Department.
Housing NOLA was listed as “Uncertified/Unapproved.”
Marked “Requires Council Legislation: No.”
Total Koch compensation: $750,000 from an out-of-state vendor, sole-sourced, flagged high risk, none through competitive procurement.
The pattern of spending public homelessness money in ways that bypass normal oversight did not begin with MRRF.
It began at the system’s redesign, with the same person who today helps set every budget line every department leader presents to Council.
And all on a contact that had a single Council sponsor.
Then District 19 Council Member Freddie O’Connell.
$2.7 million for the consulting model that explains all of this
The budget request that drew some of the least scrutiny on Wednesday deserves the most, because it reveals where Nashville’s homeless services system is heading, and whose playbook it is following.
Calvin requested $2.7 million for what she described as connecting “with downtown initiatives, MNPD, or even the nightlife outreach efforts.”
Three different things introduced as a single ask.

The line item description in the budget document tells you what this money is for, in the department’s own words: “This downtown initiative will help to increase tourism, increase city revenue, and secure safe housing options for our most chronically homeless individuals.”
Tourism first.
Revenue second.
Housing third.
When a committee member asked about it, Calvin’s answer touched every keyword without landing on a single deliverable.
She described how MNPD officers currently call OHS when they encounter someone experiencing homelessness, a phone referral that doesn’t cost $2.7 million.
She name-dropped Community Solutions, a New York-based organization that runs the Built for Zero initiative, and Clutch Consulting.
Calvin name-dropping both organizations in the same breath is not casual.
It is a signal about what the $2.7 million is for.
Clutch Consulting Group was founded by Houston’s former Special Assistant to the Mayor for Homeless Initiatives.
Their website describes a product called “Transforming Unsheltered Response” with four strategies, the third of which is titled, verbatim: “Close Downtowns to Street Sleeping.”
Their service offering includes helping communities “leverage new partners including downtowns and law enforcement to close areas to outdoor sleeping.”
The $2.7 million budget line Calvin submitted — connecting downtown initiatives, MNPD, and nightlife outreach — is the Clutch pitch deck with Nashville proper nouns swapped in.
Nashville is not listed among Clutch’s public clients, which include Dallas, Oklahoma City, New Orleans, Atlanta, Denver, Cleveland, Hartford, and Sacramento.
Either Nashville is a prospective client, or OHS is adopting the model informally, or the relationship has not been publicly disclosed.
In any case, the model is present in the budget.
Here is the thing about the Clutch model: in cities where it has been fully resourced, it appears to produce results.
Dallas reports a 19% overall reduction in homelessness and over 10,000 people rehoused.
Oklahoma City housed 126 people in its first months.
Atlanta’s Downtown Rising initiative has housed over 450 people ahead of the 2026 World Cup.

But in every one of those cities, the model was funded with significant private philanthropy alongside public dollars — Dallas had $10 million from foundations, Oklahoma City at least $5 million, Atlanta raised $156.9 million of a $235 million goal with corporate backers including Coca-Cola and Southern Company.
The model also requires dedicated landlord liaison teams, case management infrastructure, rapid onsite document processing, and published criteria for who gets housed.

In cities that adopted the model without this infrastructure, the results were different: in New Orleans, when the Tchoupitoulas encampment was closed, some residents had nowhere to go; the executive director of UNITY of Greater New Orleans called it “a primary weakness in the process.”
A man in a wheelchair with a shattered hip was told to move or face trespassing fines.
“It’s an eyesore, I don’t blame them,” he told reporters.
“But goddamn, some of us don’t have the choice of where to live.”

An encampment closed in New Orleans under the oversight of Clutch Consulting Credit: Bobbi-Jeanne Misick / Verite News
Nashville is not adopting the housing half of this model.

It is adopting the displacement half — the downtown targeting, the police coordination, the encampment closures, the coordinated entry bypass — without the private funding match, the functional landlord support systems, the governance, or the accountability that make the housing half work.
And it is doing so through a system that has already demonstrated it cannot follow the procurement rules that currently exist.
It doesn’t matter whether Clutch’s model works in Dallas or Housing First works in Finland if Nashville cannot execute a contract, verify a retention number, or produce meeting minutes.
The question is not whether these programs are effective in theory.

The question is whether giving $2.7 million to a system that made $350,000 in off-contract rent payments, that held encampment prioritization meetings in secret, that told a journalist its spending “should not be posted publicly,” will produce anything other than more of what it has already produced.
The committee member who heard all of this immediately read the subtext: “I know that they’re using private police that a lot of people are not happy with.”
Calvin did not respond to the private police reference.
The encampment decisions are being made in secret
On April 3, 2026, OHS convened the encampment prioritization team, known as PEAT, to choose which encampment to close.
I filed a public records request the same day for meeting minutes, attendee names and organizations, correspondence, and any public notice as required by the Tennessee Open Meetings Act.
TOMA requires that decisions about where government enforcement resources go constitute public meetings.
The legally mandated response deadline was April 21.
It is now May 12.
OHS has produced nothing.
If no minutes were kept and no public notice was provided, that itself may constitute a violation of state law.
I didn't file the PRR just to be an asshole.
The federal best practice , published by the U.S.

Interagency Council on Homelessness ( gutted by executive order in March 2025), is unambiguous: encampment residents are supposed to be included in discussions and decisions about their encampment, transparently and meaningfully, with a resident-selected spokesperson.
Nashville’s PEAT process is the opposite.
The meeting happens in secret.
The criteria are unpublished.
The people in the encampment are the last to know.
And it's also, as I've discussed with OHS’s Legal liaison, illegal.
Metro ethics complaints will likely be forthcoming for all those who partook in the meeting.
But secrecy is how OHS likes to do things.
“Should not be posted publicly”

When I asked Director Calvin via email to explain unauthorized rent payments I found documentation of, with the mayor and Council leadership copied, she responded: “Utilizing a dynamic process to offer urgent relief through rental assistance (bridge funding or local rapid response) from local government should not be posted publicly.”
None of those terms are terms of art.
This is big bowl of Liberal Bullshittery word salad.
They are words arranged to sound like policy while describing nothing auditable.
But the second part is plain: the director of a public office told a journalist that how public money was spent should not be posted publicly.
The mayor and Council leadership were copied.
No one objected.
Here are the facts: Every dollar in the Metro budget is subject to public records request under Tennessee law.
If a system cannot survive being described in public, the system is the problem.
The government is not, until Curtis Yarvin has his way, a corporation.
There are laws, and they say that public expenditures are subject to public oversight.
I am publishing here for the first time the actual MRRF expenditure records: the spending Calvin said “should not be posted publicly.”

These are the disbursements made under the program originally budgeted as “Non-Traditional Rapid Re-Housing,” renamed to MRRF after reporting exposed the unauthorized placements and evictions it produced.
The names of the people being served were, properly and ethically, redacted by Metro.
But the vendor names are visible for review.
