Who the system is built for

So let's get this straight:
No board, committee, or anyone else provides oversight of MRRF.
Secret encampment meetings.
A $2.7 million downtown ask with no scope of work that lists tourism before housing.
A consulting model designed for downtown business districts, imported without the infrastructure that makes it work.
A Council-mandated spending plan answered with a non-answer.
And when a journalist asked the director how the money was being spent, the answer was that it should not be posted publicly.
Each of these, individually, might be an oversight.
Together, they describe a system where the people furthest from the problem have the most control over the solution, and the people closest to it have the least.
It is possible to improve tourism and commerce and serve the unhoused.
Those goals don’t have to conflict.

But they conflict when a system unambiguously prioritizing the removal of visible homelessness from downtown corridors is presented as a system for ending homelessness, because the only thing that ends homelessness is decommodified housing, and encampment clearance optimized for business districts is not a housing program.
It is a displacement program that may or may not include housing, depending on whether the system behind it has the capacity, the criteria, and the accountability to deliver.
Nashville doesn’t.
You might assume Calvin is the bullshitter I described at the top of this piece.
Perhaps she fits the bill.
But the person I am really describing is Kristin Wilson: someone handpicked by Bloomberg Philanthropies to make cities more business-friendly while “solving street homelessness.”

Wilson’s fingerprints are on this entire architecture, from the Koch contracts to the NDP grant that attempted to funnel surveillance technology through a downtown business district to the budget that Calvin presented on Wednesday.
And the irony is that the bullshit is not even working on its own terms.
The unhoused have gained more public empathy, more political power, and more public support than ever before in modern Nashville, precisely because of what is being done to them.
The business interests Wilson was installed to serve have not been served.
They have been exposed.
The bullshit is not working.
Not for the unhoused, obviously.
But increasingly, not for the business interests it was designed to serve.
How many of you knew who Tom Turner is and what the Nashville Downtown Partnership was one year ago?
I did not.
Expect a companion piece to this on the CBID’s budget coming soon.
This is the pattern I described at the top, and it is not confined to Nashville’s homeless services budget.

The catastrophic things happening at the federal level, the gutting of agencies, the mass firings, the contempt for courts and congressional authority, were not conjured from nothing by rogue bands of alt-right operatives.
They were teed up by a generation of liberal technocrats who treated government like a business to be optimized, procurement law like a suggestion, and democratic oversight like a bottleneck.

Wilson did not need Curtis Yarvin to teach her that a city department should report to a single executive with no board oversight, that spending criteria need not be published, that encampment decisions can be made in secret, or that a journalist asking where the money went should be told it “should not be posted publicly.”

She built that architecture under two mayors, one of whom ran as “truly progressive” and now governs with a Republican chief of staff, an ICE data-pipeline builder setting the city budget, and is thrilled to have Oracle’s $4.5 billion East Bank campus rising on the riverfront.
Nashville is not a random city.

It is increasingly the playground of the billionaire class, in a state whose supermajority has gerrymandered its congressional representation, made camping on public property a felony, and systematically curtailed its capacity for democratic self-governance.
The neoliberal version of this says “run government like a business.”
The neoreactionary version says “run government like a corporation with a CEO-king.”
The difference is one of candor, not of structure.

And when the liberal version fails, when the bullshit implementations of perfectly good ideas produce declining outcomes and eroding trust, the brutal right-wing pendulum swing appears to be “the only alternative.”
That is how democracies do not fall to coups.
They are handed over, one procurement bypass at a time, by people who believed they were “innovating.”

When meeting with researchers and organizers interested in what is happening in Nashville, I have increasingly been able to tell them what my “beat” is: the intersection between the least and most powerful in our cities.
Homelessness, I’ve learned, is precisely that place.

The most powerful and politically connected, those with business interests in downtown cores and high-rise apartments they want to build and tourism they want to see grow unabated, they consistently run into the people who have been failed by our society, our economy, and our empathy.

To be able to do what you want with the bodies of the unhoused as efficiently as possible, without being hindered by complications like “what happens to them after you get them off the street,” it takes people who are able to fluently speak the liberal language of being “data-driven,” following “best practices.”

People who who are able to shield their politically motivated decisions behind “experts”, preferably experts who are not local and are therefore not accountable to having to live in the communities they are being paid to redesign.
Councilwoman Ellis asked for something she could explain to a group of kids at a bus stop.
Here it is: Nashville spent $50 million to reduce homelessness.
Homelessness went up.
The people in charge said different things to different rooms about why.
Sometimes, different things are in the same room.
And the system is built so that no one with the power to ask the next question has the information needed to do so.
The system is not built for the people it is meant to serve.
It is built for the people who find those-who-need-housing to be inconvenient, not for the people who need housing.

The city would rather throw good money after bad, pouring it directly into the pockets of the landlords who are emptying people onto our streets, than actually invest in the thing that would solve it: decommodified housing.
I don’t think they will do it.
And here is why: They will not do it because it doesn’t make people money.
It's not that they won’t make money from it, it's not corruption in that straight forward a way.
But actually providing housing as a human right, not making it a commodity that someone can extract vast wealth from, goes against their core beliefs.
Doing something that does not make people money is dangerous to them because it would show that the world they think they live in is a lie.
At the core of the belief that seems to unite the Far Right and the Centrist Liberals who run Nashville is the conviction that might makes right.
The only difference is in its application.
To the Far Right, power should be exercised through brutal, dominating, violent force.

To Centrist Liberals, power is meant to be exerted secretively — through obfuscation of methods, the usurping of norms, and the abstraction of process until the less powerful become the least powerful and the most confused.
What the Centrist Liberals seem not to realize, or do not care about, is that this is precisely the architecture that has led to the violent takeover of our democracy by the Far Right.

This is precisely the world that Curtis Yarvin has been calling for — renaming the God Emperor, with power of life and death over all his subjects, in the euphemistic terms of "CEO" of a corporate state.
This is, quite literally, the definition of fascism, and Centrist Liberals have been designing its instruments for decades.
In Nashville, they have been doing it most of all to precisely the targets who were the first victims of last century's fascists: the unhoused, the disenfranchised, and the unconventional.

In June 1938, Reinhard Heydrich ordered a nationwide raid that sent 9,500 people labeled "asocial" to Buchenwald, Dachau, and Sachsenhausen — most of them homeless, beggars, welfare recipients, and casual workers; the Nazi regime regarded homeless people, along with those unable to hold a job, as "genetically degenerate" threats to the so-called health of the race.
I don’t know how to make this clearer: a system that is unaccountable, ungovernable, untransparent, and unambiguously failing at the very thing it’s supposed to do is always dangerous and bad.

But in the current political climate, it is, and I truly do not believe I am exaggerating, the recipe for having people “disappear”, for sex trafficking, for corpses sold for profit, and, if history repeats itself, mass murder.
And if that does not concern you, please…
just think of the legal liability that might create for Metro Nashville and the businesses associated with the activities downtown.
Maybe that’ll make you care?
Director Calvin is right: the solution to homelessness is housing.
She is unquestionably correct.

If Nashville actually provided what even she knows is needed (decommodified housing), all of this mishegoss of paying slumlords, pretending we’re Housing First, millions in consulting contracts to wrest control of the continuum of care from the people who actually do the work, all of it would be shown for what it really is.
Liberal bullshittery.

Staff Investigative Report 
June 26, 2026 
I.

Introduction 
This report presents the findings of the Metropolitan Human Relations Commission ("MHRC") 
staff following an investigation into allegations concerning the administration of federally-
funded housing assistance and housing stabilization services by the Metropolitan Government of 
Nashville and Davidson County Office of Homeless Services ("OHS").

The investigation was 
conducted pursuant to the Commission's authority under the Metropolitan Charter, the 
Metropolitan Code of Laws, the Commission's Rules and Procedures, and applicable federal civil 
rights laws governing recipients of federal financial assistance.

The investigation concerns allegations that OHS, in administering bridge housing placements, 
rental assistance, housing navigation services, and access to permanent housing resources, may 
have employed inconsistent or inadequately-defined policies and practices that resulted in 
unequal treatment or a disparate impact on protected classes, particularly Black women and 
women of color experiencing homelessness.

The allegations arise from complaints submitted to the Commission, documentary evidence 
obtained during the investigation, interviews with complainants, current and former service 
providers, former OHS personnel, and other witnesses possessing relevant information regarding 
the administration of these programs.

The purpose of this report is not to determine ultimate liability or make findings equivalent to 
those rendered by a court of law.

Rather, consistent with Rule 2.7 of the MHRC Rules and 
Procedures, this report evaluates whether sufficient evidence exists to establish probable cause to 
believe that an unlawful discriminatory practice may have occurred, thereby warranting further 
proceedings, including conciliation.
II.

Jurisdiction 
The Metropolitan Human Relations Commission is authorized to investigate allegations of 
unlawful discrimination within its jurisdiction, including discrimination arising from the 
administration of federally-assisted programs and activities.

At all times relevant to this investigation, the Office of Homeless Services administered or 
coordinated programs supported through federal financial assistance, including funding 
authorized under the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), U.S.

Department of Housing and 
Urban Development (HUD) programs, Continuum of Care (CoC) funding, Emergency Solutions 
Grant (ESG) funding, and other federal and local housing initiatives.

OHS exercised substantial 
authority over participant selection, housing placement, funding allocation, housing navigation, 
rental assistance administration, and coordination with nonprofit service providers participating 
in federally-funded homelessness response systems.

Because these programs were administered with federal financial assistance, they are subject to 
the nondiscrimination requirements of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and its 
implementing regulations, which prohibit discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national 
origin in programs receiving federal financial assistance, as well as state and local law and 
policy.

Accordingly, MHRC possesses jurisdiction to investigate whether the administration of these 
federally assisted housing programs complied with applicable civil rights requirements.
III.

The investigation also examined whether OHS maintained objective standards governing these 
decisions and whether such standards were applied consistently across similarly situated 
participants.

Although the investigation includes the experiences of individual complainants and witnesses, 
the inquiry is not limited to the circumstances of any single participant.

Rather, the investigation 
evaluates whether the design or administration of the relevant programs resulted in systemic 
inequities affecting participants receiving federally funded housing services.
IV.

Allegations 
The investigation was conducted to determine whether the evidence supports the following 
findings: 
1.

Whether OHS administered federally funded housing programs pursuant to written policies, 
objective eligibility criteria, and consistently applied procedures governing participant selection, 
rental assistance, and housing transitions.

Whether participants for bridge housing, rental assistance, and housing navigation services 
were selected using transparent, documented, and consistently applied criteria, including whether 
Coordinated Entry tools or standardized prioritization systems were uniformly utilized.

Whether participants received accurate, consistent, and complete information regarding 
duration of rental assistance, eligibility for housing vouchers, and pathways to permanent 
housing.

Whether modifications to rental assistance or participant financial obligations were 
implemented pursuant to established policies, and whether such changes were consistently 
communicated and documented.

Whether OHS maintained adequate documentation supporting participant selection, 
prioritization decisions, voucher referrals, program exits, and rental assistance determinations.

Whether similarly-situated participants received different treatment with respect to housing 
placement, rental assistance, voucher access, or program continuation without documented 
justification.

Whether facially-neutral policies or practices governing shelter exits, housing placement, and 
rental assistance had a disproportionate adverse impact on protected classes, including Black 
women and women of color experiencing homelessness.

Whether the totality of the evidence supports a reasonable basis to believe that the 
administration of federally funded housing programs by OHS may have violated Title VI or 
related nondiscrimination requirements.
V.

Standard of Review 
Pursuant to Rule 2.7 of the MHRC Rules and Procedures, the purpose of an investigation is to 
determine whether probable cause exists to believe that an unlawful discriminatory practice may 
have occurred.
Probable cause is a threshold determination.

It does not require proof by a preponderance of the 
evidence or proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

Rather, the inquiry is whether the evidence, 
viewed as a whole, provides a reasonable basis to believe that unlawful discrimination may have 
occurred and that further proceedings are warranted.

Where evidence was conflicting, staff evaluated credibility based upon corroboration, 
consistency, documentary support, contemporaneous records, and the plausibility of each 
account when considered in context of the entire investigative record.

No adverse inference was drawn solely from disputed testimony where documentary evidence 
remained incomplete or unavailable.
VI.

Documents Reviewed and Witnesses Interviewed 
3

The investigation included review of documentary records, communications, policies, contracts, 
and funding materials obtained from the parties and third parties, as well as interviews with 
complainants, current and former employees of participating organizations, and former OHS 
personnel, housing providers, and other individuals possessing relevant knowledge.

Investigators also examined publicly available information concerning the operation of 
Nashville's homelessness response system, Continuum of Care requirements, HUD guidance, 
applicable grant requirements, and demographic information relevant to the administration of 
homeless services.

Where appropriate, investigative findings were evaluated against nationally recognized 
principles governing equitable administration of federally funded programs and the requirements 
of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
VIII.

Background Information 
The Office of Homeless Services ("OHS") serves as Metropolitan Nashville and Davidson 
County's lead agency for coordinating the local response to homelessness.

During the period 
relevant to this investigation, OHS administered, coordinated, or oversaw numerous housing and 
homelessness initiatives funded through a combination of federal, state, local, and private 
resources.

Among its responsibilities, OHS coordinated emergency shelter operations, housing navigation, 
landlord engagement, rental assistance, supportive services, homeless management information 
systems, and the administration of federal grants intended to increase access to stable housing for 
individuals and families experiencing homelessness.

OHS also served as a central coordinating entity among nonprofit service providers, property 
owners, housing developers, and governmental partners participating in Nashville's homelessness 
response system.

Because many of these activities were supported through federal financial assistance, OHS was 
required to administer its programs in accordance with applicable federal civil rights 
requirements, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Nashville participates in HUD's Continuum of Care ("CoC") program, which is intended to 
create a coordinated system for addressing homelessness through community-wide planning, 
prioritization, and allocation of housing resources.

As part of the CoC framework, participating agencies utilize a Coordinated Entry process 
designed to assess individuals and families experiencing homelessness, evaluate vulnerability 
and housing needs, and prioritize participants for available housing resources.

The Coordinated Entry system is intended to promote consistency, transparency, and equitable 
access by reducing reliance upon informal referrals or subjective decision-making.

Under this 
framework, participants are generally assessed using standardized tools and referred to available 
4

housing resources according to established prioritization criteria, while recognizing that certain 
funding streams or specialized programs may have additional eligibility requirements.

The effectiveness of Coordinated Entry depends upon the consistent application of objective 
criteria and accurate documentation of participant assessments, referrals, and program status1.

The demographic composition of the population served by Nashville's homelessness response 
system provides important context for evaluating the potential impact of administrative 
decisions.

Nationally, Black individuals and families are disproportionately represented among people 
experiencing homelessness despite comprising a substantially smaller percentage of the overall 
population2.

Research has consistently shown that Black families, particularly Black women with 
children, are overrepresented among households utilizing emergency shelters and family shelter 
systems3.

Available national outreach data and point-in-time count similarly indicate that families residing 
in Nashville's emergency shelters include a disproportionately high percentage of Black residents 
and other people of color4.

By contrast, outreach data and point-in-time counts have often shown 
a comparatively higher proportion of unsheltered individuals living in encampments who 
identify as White, although demographic patterns vary over time and by location.
These demographic realities do not establish discrimination.

They do, however, underscore why 
decisions affecting access to shelter exits, bridge housing, rental assistance, and permanent 
housing opportunities warrant careful examination under Title VI when the affected participant 
population is disproportionately composed of members of protected classes.
IX.

Factual Findings 
1.

The Office of Homeless Services (OHS) administered and/or coordinated federally funded 
housing and homelessness response programs during the period August 2024 through August 
2025, including programs supported by ARPA and related funding streams.

OHS partnered with nonprofit service providers, including Step Up and others, to implement 
housing placement, rental assistance, and housing navigation services.

5

Participants in the program at issue were primarily individuals and families experiencing 
homelessness who had previously been residing in emergency shelter, namely the Nashville 
Rescue Mission.

Participants were placed into apartment units at properties including The Ave and Hillside 
Crossing under arrangements involving OHS, service providers, and property managers.

The initiative involved a combination of housing placement, rental assistance, and supportive 
services intended to stabilize participants and transition them toward permanent housing.

Eight families were selected for placement at The Ave and Hillside Crossing from emergency 
shelter populations, including individuals experiencing “overflow” conditions at the Nashville 
Rescue Mission.

Witness testimony indicates that participants were informed they were being moved into 
housing with supportive services intended to facilitate long-term stability.

The investigation has not yet obtained complete documentation demonstrating the specific 
criteria used to select individual participants for placement in the initiative.

(OHS has not 
responded to requests regarding this finding) 
9.

The record contains conflicting accounts regarding whether standardized Coordinated Entry 
prioritization tools were used to select all participants for placement.

Witnesses report that OHS or its partners initially represented that rental assistance would be 
provided for a defined period, including references to approximately one year of rent support in 
certain cases.

Participants later experienced reductions in rental assistance obligations, including transitions 
toward increased tenant responsibility for rent payments.

Multiple witnesses reported that, during late 2024 through 2025, OHS and/or partner 
agencies discussed changes to rental assistance structure due to funding constraints.

Witness testimony describes the development of a phased rent reduction or “breakdown 
plan” under which participant rent obligations increased over time while program subsidies 
decreased.
Participants were subsequently notified of increased rent obligations during 2025.

Several participants reported receiving lease violation notices, eviction notices, or rent 
demands following reductions in rental assistance.

Participants described the changes in rent obligations as destabilizing and inconsistent with 
their understanding of the terms under which they entered the program.
Two of the eight participants did not obtain housing vouchers.

The investigation has not yet received complete documentation identifying the written 
policies governing participant selection, rental assistance duration, or program exit criteria for 
the initiative.

Multiple witnesses described variations in how policies were communicated and applied 
across participants and providers.

The record reflects gaps in documentation regarding how individual participant decisions 
were made, including selection and prioritization decisions.

A former Step Up employee reported concerns regarding changes in program administration, 
including rental assistance practices and participant treatment.

The same witness reported being asked to revise a written statement and declining to do so 
based on professional ethics.
The witness subsequently resigned from employment with Step Up.

Witnesses reported internal communications emphasizing alignment or “unity” with OHS 
leadership in the context of provider advocacy concerns.

Participants affected by the program at issue include a substantial proportion of Black 
women and women of color, consistent with demographic patterns of families experiencing 
sheltered homelessness in Nashville.

National research indicates that Black households, particularly Black women with children, 
are disproportionately represented in sheltered homelessness populations compared to their share 
of the general population.6 
X.

Findings on Allegations and Probable Cause Determination 
Based on the Findings of Fact set forth in Section IX, MHRC staff makes the following 
determinations as to each allegation: 
1.

Whether OHS administered federally-funded housing programs pursuant to written 
policies, objective eligibility criteria, and consistently applied procedures governing 
participant selection, rental assistance, and housing transitions.

7

The investigation finds that OHS has not produced complete written policies governing 
participant selection, rental assistance duration, or housing transition criteria for the initiative at 
issue.

Whether participants for bridge housing, rental assistance, and housing navigation 
services were selected using transparent, documented, and consistently applied criteria, 
including whether Coordinated Entry tools or standardized prioritization systems were 
uniformly utilized.

The investigation finds that participants were selected from emergency shelter populations, 
including overflow populations from the Nashville Rescue Mission.

The record does not 
establish that standardized Coordinated Entry tools or documented prioritization criteria were 
uniformly applied to all participants.

Whether participants received accurate, consistent, and complete information regarding: 
duration of rental assistance, eligibility for housing vouchers, and pathways to 
permanent housing.

The investigation finds the conflicting accounts regarding the information provided to 
participants concerning.

Whether modifications to rental assistance or participant financial obligations were 
implemented pursuant to established policies, and whether such changes were 
consistently communicated and documented.

The investigation finds that participants experienced reductions in rental assistance obligations 
and/or increases in tenant responsibility during 2025.

Witness testimony indicates these changes 
may have been implemented in response to funding concerns and were not consistently 
communicated across all participants.

Whether OHS maintained adequate documentation supporting: participant selection, 
prioritization decisions, voucher referrals, program exits, and rental assistance 
determinations.

The investigation finds that OHS has failed to produce any written documentation nor responded 
to the multiple attempts to obtain answers to these questions.

Whether similarly situated participants received different treatment with respect to 
housing placement, rental assistance, voucher access, or program continuation without 
documented justification.

The investigation finds that similarly situated participants experienced different outcomes with 
respect to rental assistance adjustments and housing transition outcomes.

Whether facially neutral policies or practices governing shelter exits, housing placement, 
and rental assistance had a disproportionate adverse impact on protected classes, 
including Black women and women of color experiencing homelessness.

The investigation finds that the affected population includes a substantial proportion of Black 
women and women of color, shelter-based housing interventions disproportionately affect these 
populations nationally; and the challenged practices govern access to shelter exits, housing 
stability, and the 8 women and their children affected by OHS’s practices were 
disproportionately Black and women of color.

Whether the totality of the evidence supports a reasonable basis to believe that the 
administration of federally funded housing programs by OHS may have violated Title VI 
or related nondiscrimination requirements.

Based on the totality of the evidence, the investigation finds that there is a probable cause to 
believe that OHS’s administration of federally-funded housing programs did not comply with 
Title VI requirements.

Issuing Department: Office of Homeless Services (OHS)
Overview
The Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County, through the Office of Homeless Services (OHS), is seeking proposals from qualified nonprofit organizations to provide administrative, financial, and coordination support for the Nashville/Davidson County Continuum of Care’s (CoC) Consumer Advisory Board (CAB), also known as the Lived Experience Cohort, and Youth Action Board (YAB).

These advisory boards are composed of individuals with lived experience of homelessness and play a critical role in informing Continuum of Care (CoC) policies, programming, priorities, and strategic planning.
The selected vendor will help to ensure meaningful participation by administering stipends, coordinating operations, and supporting onboarding, recruitment, and reporting functions.

Purpose
The purpose of this Request for Proposals is to select an organization that will support and compensate individuals with lived experience of homelessness to participate in the Continuum of Care’s CAB and YAB.
The CAB and YAB function as advisory bodies by providing insights and recommendations to the Homelessness Planning Council (HPC) and the CoC.

The Continuum of Care and the Office of Homeless Services recognize that people with lived experience offer unique perspectives and expertise on the realities of housing instability and navigating Nashville’s homeless response system.
The insight of people with lived experience can help our Continuum of Care improve how programs are designed, how policies are developed, and how services are delivered.

Because of this, the CoC and the Collaborative Applicant aim to restore compensation and meaningful engagement of people with lived experience by way of the CAB and YAB to inform CoC policies, programs, and strategies.

Background
The Nashville/Davidson County Continuum of Care
The Continuum of Care (CoC) is Nashville’s planning body responsible for coordinating the funding and delivery of housing and services for people experiencing homelessness.

The mission of the Continuum of Care is to create a collaborative, inclusive, community-based process and approach to planning and managing effective homeless assistance resources and programs (by which Federal, State and local funding resources will be used to fund all homelessness assistance needs) to end homelessness in our community, consistent with 24 CFR Part 578, the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) regulations that guide the CoC program.
The Nashville-Davidson County Continuum of Care is made up of a General Membership of community partners and individuals dedicated to ending homelessness in Nashville.
The Homelessness Planning Council is the governance board for the Nashville-Davidson County Continuum of Care, responsible for guiding CoC operations, strategic planning, and policies.

Issuing Agency
The Office of Homeless Services’ mission is to lead Nashville’s efforts to end homelessness through innovation, community collaboration, and compassion.

OHS works closely with government agencies, nonprofit providers, healthcare partners, and other community partners to strengthen the local homelessness response system and improve outcomes for people experiencing homelessness.
In addition to coordinating programs and funding, OHS plays several key leadership roles within the local system.
The department serves as the lead agency for the Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) and Coordinated Entry, supporting consistent data collection and fair access to housing and services.

OHS also provides staff and resources to the Homelessness Planning Council, the governing body of the local Continuum of Care, and in November 2023 was designated by CoC membership as the community’s Collaborative Applicant, responsible for coordinating and submitting the region’s federal CoC funding applications to the U.S.
Department of Housing and Urban Development.
Through these roles, OHS helps align public resources, provider efforts, and community partnerships to prevent and end homelessness in Nashville and Davidson County.

Consumer Advisory Board and Youth Action Board
The Consumer Advisory Board (CAB), also known as the Lived Experience Cohort, is a group of people with lived experience of homelessness who advise and inform the Nashville-Davidson County Continuum of Care.

The CAB strives to ensure that local efforts to end homelessness and support unhoused residents are centered around the needs, desires, and unique perspectives of those who have experienced homelessness in Nashville-Davidson County.
The Youth Action Board (YAB) is the CAB’s counterpart for individuals aged 18 to 24 who have experienced homelessness as children, teens, or young adults.
The CAB and YAB were originally established as committees of the Homelessness Planning Council.

This structure proposed challenges when the Office of Homeless Services assumed the role of the Collaborative Applicant, as the Metro Charter does not allow any type of compensation related to service on a Metro board or a committee thereof.
In February 2026, the CoC voted to move the CAB and YAB under the purview of the General Membership.

At this juncture, the Office of Homeless Services is seeking a non-profit organization to serve as the fiscal agent to compensate individuals experiencing homelessness with funds from the Continuum of Care Planning Grant.

Anticipated Contract Term
The anticipated term length for this contract is one year.
Opportunities for contract renewal will be dependent on funding availability and vendor performance.

Scope of Work
The selected contractor will handle day-to-day administration for the CAB and YAB, including managing stipends, supporting members, and managing timesheets.
The goal is to keep board operations running smoothly, with clear processes, timely payments, and alignment with Continuum of Care priorities.

· Develop a compensation plan in collaboration with CAB and YAB members, aligned with Metro and CoC policies
· Process stipends and reimbursements in a timely and accurate manner
· Review and approve CAB and YAB timesheets, attendance records, and meeting minutes to verify payments align with participation and contributions
· Maintain financial records and payment tracking systems
· Provide regular payout summaries and financial reports to the Office of Homeless Services for grant reporting
· Ensure compliance with all applicable tax regulations and grant requirements
· Provide clear guidance and support to members regarding payment processes
· Resolve payment issues promptly and provide adequate documentation to the Office of Homeless Services
· Provide documents and reports as needed to Metro, in compliance with Metro grant policies and procedures
· Undertake annual monitoring activities executed by the Office of Homeless Services
2.

CAB and YAB Support and Alignment
· Participate in meetings with CAB and YAB regarding governance, policies, and support needs
· Coordinate with national lived experience organizations, including the National Alliance to End Homelessness, to align efforts with best practices, as needed
· Communicate with CAB and YAB chairs on a regular basis to identify support needs and promote alignment with the Continuum of Care
· Coordinate with the Office of Homeless Services to address CAB and YAB needs and concerns
3.

Membership and Orientation
· Support the General Membership, CAB, and YAB in creating fair processes for selecting new members
· Develop onboarding materials, including welcome packets, program overviews, and policies
· Coordinate and facilitate orientation sessions, including training on roles, responsibilities, and the Continuum of Care, as needed
· Ensure members understand participation expectations and compensation processes
Deliverables
The selected vendor will provide, at minimum:

· Onboarding materials

Learn More About Recent Homelessness Updates out of Nashville
By Judith Tackett | August 5, 2026

Like Tweet Email Print
More
• Subscribe to Features
Over the past few weeks, there have been some relevant homelessness updates in Nashville:
• Metro Council passed the Metro Budget for Fiscal Year 2027, significantly increasing the budget of the Office of Homelessness Services (OHS);
• OHS released the 2026 State of Homelessness Community Report;
• The Metro Human Relations Committee completed an initial investigation about a Title VI complaint against the OHS that found probable cause for discrimination; and
• OHS finally released the long-awaited Consumer Advisory Board Request for Proposal (RFP) to pay people with lived experience for their contributions.
• I will take these issues one-by-one.
OHS Sees Increase in Metro FY27 Budget
The Office of Homeless Services’ (OHS’) current FY27 budget, which runs from July 1, 2026­­ — June 30, 2027, is about $18.5 million.
Of that total, $17,233,600 is from the General Services District (GSD) budget, which supports government operations and is generated mostly from property and sales taxes.
The remaining $1,277,600 was budgeted under the Special Purpose Fund (SPF), which stems from grants or donations for a specific purpose.
The Mayor’s recommended budget originally included $15,683,600 in GSD funding, which Metro Council ended up increasing by $1.55 million.

Added expenses include a $1.25 million grant to the Hospitality Hub to continue running a temporary housing program out of a motel in South Nashville and $300,000 to Launch Pad, a youth/young adult service provider.
(You can read up on OHS’ original budget request in our June 3, 2026 issue.)
The final budget allocation to OHS is 48 percent, or $5.6 million, more than the FY26 budget.

I appreciate the increase in the budget, though I remain critical of Metro’s leadership on homelessness and feel strongly that changes in the Mayor’s Office and at OHS are needed to use those dollars to benefit people experiencing homelessness more effectively to benefit more people in need.
OHS’ State of Homelessness Report Raises Questions
In June, shortly after Metro Council increased its budget from $11.6 million last year to $17.2 million in the current fiscal year, OHS held the 2026 State of Homelessness Symposium.
At that event, OHS released a community report chock full of data points.

In some of my recent columns, I strongly criticized OHS’ use and presentation of data, stating that data reports published by the Office of Homeless Services are contradictory, confusing or plain false in some cases.
Metro’s State of Homelessness Report reinforced my opinion.
The report raises more questions than it answers and is a hugely missed opportunity to start open and transparent conversations.
The report leaves me with quite a few questions.
Why does OHS keep presenting output numbers as impact data?

For example, on Page 5, OHS presents a 2025 HMIS Data Report and includes “System Impact Indicators” at the bottom, which in fact present population snapshots and do not show any structural changes or shifts over time.
Then, on Page 11, OHS outlined the “ARPA Impact,” which specifically focuses on the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding, which, according to the presented data, totaled about $52.5 million.
After adding up each of the allocations, I found that their total amount of $52,467,033 listed on Page 12 was off by $2.62.
You may say that that’s just a couple of dollars, but these simple math mistakes make me wonder about their editing process.

In actuality, their total may have been off by another $2.8 million because OHS omitted the fact that the developer of Shelby House 1, LP, returned their entire allocation after working with OHS to house 14 individuals in some of those units.
There is also no mention in the report of what happened to those $2.8 million and why they were still included in the $52.5 million “impact” report.

I have asked Metro what happened to the money, and OHS responded that “the $2.8 million returned by Shelby House was reallocated through Metro’s approved process to three priorities: Eviction Right to Counsel as a homelessness-prevention and diversion strategy, permanent funding for critical positions previously supported by ARPA within the Office of Homeless Services, and permanent funding for critical ARPA-supported positions within the Office of Family Safety.”
I have voiced my concerns to OHS three times now, first in early April, following up in May and most recently in preparation for this column.
I specifically asked why corrections were not made.
OHS said that “Shelby House received an allocation from APRA funding but should not have been included on this page.”
They did not respond to my question about why output numbers are presented as impact throughout this report.
When a report lists how many services were provided (outputs), we won’t know whether that truly reduced homelessness over time (impact).
This information does not tell us anything about the kind of services that were provided, how effective they were, where we see gaps in our local homelessness response, etc.
Here are some of the many questions I have:
• Of the 1,599 individuals OHS says moved into permanent housing under the ARPA grants, how many are still housed?
• Of the 888 individuals connected to interim housing, how many moved on to permanent housing, and how many are they still there?
• And why would OHS say that 735 housing units were developed, including 168 units for people experiencing homelessness?
Why not just list the 168 units as the main output that this money generated?
And were the 14 units from Shelby House 1, LP deducted from the 168 number?

OHS had an opportunity to go back to the drawing board and review these output numbers but chose to repeat this misleading information to Metro Council in their budget presentation in May and also include it in the 2026 State of Homelessness Report.
OHS states in the report that, “In three years, Nashville has successfully relocated over 500 people from eight outdoor encampments into permanent housing, interim housing or family reunification.”
This directly contradicts two previously published reports and statements from OHS.
Based on February data reported to Metro Council, 341 people resided in seven encampments that were closed.
And in a December sworn affidavit to a federal judge, OHS Director April Calvin wrote, “…
seven encampments across Davidson County have closed over the course of the last four years.
Those encampments had a total population of approximately five hundred residents,…”
I asked OHS whether there was an encampment closure of 100-150 people since February 2026 that I may have missed.
OHS answered that “The eight encampments referenced in the report include the Jefferson Street encampment.
The cumulative total covers a three-year period and does not indicate that an encampment of 100 to 150 people was closed between February and June 2026.”

The fact is that the Jefferson Street encampment could have been included in those previous reports since it was closed in early 2022 and certainly had far fewer than 100 people living there at the time of closure.
Unfortunately, these are not even close to all of the examples of contradictory, misleading and incorrect information I found in Metro’s 2026 State of Homelessness Community Report.
Everyone makes mistakes.

But to me, the consistency and continuity of the mistakes, even after being pointed out, strongly indicates that Metro homelessness leaders are more about elevating their own image than truly analyzing available data in an honest and transparent way that would allow us, as a community, to examine where we need to invest the millions of dollars that Metro continues to have at its disposal.
Metro Human Relations Commission Report Finds Probable Cause that OHS may have Discriminated Against Minorities
At the end of June, the Metro Human Relations Commission (MHRC) released an investigative report that examined a Title VI complaint against the Office of Homeless Services (OHS).
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national origin in programs.

The MHRC report was extremely detailed and outlined the full accusation and essentially concluded that there is probable cause that OHS discriminated against people who belong to a minority population.

In his letter to OHS, his board, and others, MHRC Executive Director Davie Tucker wrote, “Based upon the Staff Investigative Report and my independent review, I hereby determine that there is probable cause to believe that the administration of federally funded housing assistance and housing stabilization programs by the Office of Homeless Services resulted in inconsistent application of policies and practices that had a disproportionate adverse effect on Black women and women of color, in a manner that warrants further proceedings under Rule 2.7 of the MHRC Rules and Procedures.
Accordingly, this complaint is upheld, and will advance to a formal conciliation process.”
Tucker’s letter also outlines a timeline that shows how unresponsive OHS was to requests from MHRC during this initial investigation.
The next step is conciliation, meaning that there will be a remediation attempt to eliminate the alleged discriminatory practice.

Tucker is also clear in his letter that “probable cause is not a finding of guilt, it is a higher standard than reasonable suspicion and demands a higher degree of certainty and fair probability that evidence of discrimination will be found.
Nothing in this Determination constitutes a final finding of discrimination or liability.”
Consumer Advisory Board (CAB) Payments RFP Now Open After Delay
When people in the human services field talk about paying people with lived experience for their participation, it is about acknowledging the value and expertise of these individuals.
Furthermore, people with lived experience and expertise often do not get paid for their time when we invite them to the table to solicit their input — while others are paid through their day jobs.

I asked OHS to help us understand why they stopped paying the Continuum of Care (Coc) Consumer Advisory Board (CAB) with the federal planning dollars, a direct grant from the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), that OHS receives on behalf of the community and that could be used for paying CAB members.

Here is the response, “When the Office of Homeless Services became the Collaborative Applicant for the Nashville Continuum of Care, Metro Charter provisions governing Metro Boards and Commissions applied to the Homelessness Planning Council and its committees.
As a result, OHS could no longer directly compensate individuals serving on those committees.

To establish a compensation process consistent with Metro requirements, OHS issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) to identify an independent organization to administer compensation for members of the Consumer Advisory Board (CAB) and Youth Action Board (YAB).”
After months of delays, that RFP is finally posted at https://www.nashville.gov/departments/office-homeless-services/continuum-care/current-rfp and open until July 31.
There is a lot of homelessness-specific terminology in the OHS statement that I won’t break down this time.
But as a former long-term Metro employee, I can confirm that Metro makes it very difficult to pay people with lived experience who sit on a board or on a committee.
In general, Metro, by law, cannot pay board/commission members.
The problem, however, is that in this instance:

• CAB members who asked for remediation of this situation for over a year did not request any payments for people sitting on the Homelessness Planning Council (HPC), which is the decision-making body of the Continuum of Care (CoC).
The CoC is composed of community stakeholders working together to build a homeless crisis response system.
• The HPC functions as the CoC Board and therefore, is a community board that happens to sit within Metro after it was combined with the Metropolitan Homelessness Commission in 2018.
But, the HPC is not your typical Metro board because the HPC has absolutely no power over Metro resources (neither the OHS budget, nor the final hiring or firing decision of HPC staff).
Their primary purpose is “to secure and manage federal funding, oversee the local homeless response system, and ensure compliance with HUD regulations.
• The only dollars over which the HPC has direct oversight are the Planning dollars managed by OHS as the Collaborative Applicant (a term the essential refers to the selected Lead Agency of the CoC).
• CoC committees, including the CAB and YAB, are not decision-making bodies as they only make recommendations to the HPC (see point 1).

My main question therefore is: how is it that Metro, including OHS, can hire multiple consultants through single-source contracts, but they cannot figure out what needs to be done to hire CAB and YAB members as independent contractors with the task to advise the HPC and the CoC?
Why All of This Matters
Taking a critical view of Metro’s approach to homelessness is necessary because the city is overseeing the largest funding pot ($18.5 million) to help some of our most vulnerable neighbors.
OHS touts to be data-driven.
But their data tells me they are output-driven and focus more on propaganda than using data for actual needs analysis.
I also believe that OHS has the potential because OHS has the resources at their disposal.
But OHS does not have the trust of the community or, seemingly, the will to build that trust.
We, as a city, can and should do better than what we have seen over the past few years.
Source documents, including the 2026 State of Homelessness Community Report and the two MHRC reports, will be linked to in our online version of this article.
Judith Tackett is a longtime homelessness expert and advocate for housing-focused, person-centered solutions.
Opinions in this column are her own.

Learn More About Recent Homelessness Updates out of Nashville
By Judith Tackett | August 5, 2026

Like Tweet Email Print
More
• Subscribe to Features
Over the past few weeks, there have been some relevant homelessness updates in Nashville:
• Metro Council passed the Metro Budget for Fiscal Year 2027, significantly increasing the budget of the Office of Homelessness Services (OHS);
• OHS released the 2026 State of Homelessness Community Report;
• The Metro Human Relations Committee completed an initial investigation about a Title VI complaint against the OHS that found probable cause for discrimination; and
• OHS finally released the long-awaited Consumer Advisory Board Request for Proposal (RFP) to pay people with lived experience for their contributions.
• I will take these issues one-by-one.
OHS Sees Increase in Metro FY27 Budget
The Office of Homeless Services’ (OHS’) current FY27 budget, which runs from July 1, 2026­­ — June 30, 2027, is about $18.5 million.
Of that total, $17,233,600 is from the General Services District (GSD) budget, which supports government operations and is generated mostly from property and sales taxes.
The remaining $1,277,600 was budgeted under the Special Purpose Fund (SPF), which stems from grants or donations for a specific purpose.
The Mayor’s recommended budget originally included $15,683,600 in GSD funding, which Metro Council ended up increasing by $1.55 million.

Added expenses include a $1.25 million grant to the Hospitality Hub to continue running a temporary housing program out of a motel in South Nashville and $300,000 to Launch Pad, a youth/young adult service provider.
(You can read up on OHS’ original budget request in our June 3, 2026 issue.)
The final budget allocation to OHS is 48 percent, or $5.6 million, more than the FY26 budget.

I appreciate the increase in the budget, though I remain critical of Metro’s leadership on homelessness and feel strongly that changes in the Mayor’s Office and at OHS are needed to use those dollars to benefit people experiencing homelessness more effectively to benefit more people in need.
OHS’ State of Homelessness Report Raises Questions
In June, shortly after Metro Council increased its budget from $11.6 million last year to $17.2 million in the current fiscal year, OHS held the 2026 State of Homelessness Symposium.
At that event, OHS released a community report chock full of data points.

In some of my recent columns, I strongly criticized OHS’ use and presentation of data, stating that data reports published by the Office of Homeless Services are contradictory, confusing or plain false in some cases.
Metro’s State of Homelessness Report reinforced my opinion.
The report raises more questions than it answers and is a hugely missed opportunity to start open and transparent conversations.
The report leaves me with quite a few questions.
Why does OHS keep presenting output numbers as impact data?

For example, on Page 5, OHS presents a 2025 HMIS Data Report and includes “System Impact Indicators” at the bottom, which in fact present population snapshots and do not show any structural changes or shifts over time.
Then, on Page 11, OHS outlined the “ARPA Impact,” which specifically focuses on the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding, which, according to the presented data, totaled about $52.5 million.
After adding up each of the allocations, I found that their total amount of $52,467,033 listed on Page 12 was off by $2.62.
You may say that that’s just a couple of dollars, but these simple math mistakes make me wonder about their editing process.

In actuality, their total may have been off by another $2.8 million because OHS omitted the fact that the developer of Shelby House 1, LP, returned their entire allocation after working with OHS to house 14 individuals in some of those units.
There is also no mention in the report of what happened to those $2.8 million and why they were still included in the $52.5 million “impact” report.

I have asked Metro what happened to the money, and OHS responded that “the $2.8 million returned by Shelby House was reallocated through Metro’s approved process to three priorities: Eviction Right to Counsel as a homelessness-prevention and diversion strategy, permanent funding for critical positions previously supported by ARPA within the Office of Homeless Services, and permanent funding for critical ARPA-supported positions within the Office of Family Safety.”
I have voiced my concerns to OHS three times now, first in early April, following up in May and most recently in preparation for this column.
I specifically asked why corrections were not made.
OHS said that “Shelby House received an allocation from APRA funding but should not have been included on this page.”
They did not respond to my question about why output numbers are presented as impact throughout this report.
When a report lists how many services were provided (outputs), we won’t know whether that truly reduced homelessness over time (impact).
This information does not tell us anything about the kind of services that were provided, how effective they were, where we see gaps in our local homelessness response, etc.
Here are some of the many questions I have:
• Of the 1,599 individuals OHS says moved into permanent housing under the ARPA grants, how many are still housed?
• Of the 888 individuals connected to interim housing, how many moved on to permanent housing, and how many are they still there?
• And why would OHS say that 735 housing units were developed, including 168 units for people experiencing homelessness?
Why not just list the 168 units as the main output that this money generated?
And were the 14 units from Shelby House 1, LP deducted from the 168 number?

OHS had an opportunity to go back to the drawing board and review these output numbers but chose to repeat this misleading information to Metro Council in their budget presentation in May and also include it in the 2026 State of Homelessness Report.
OHS states in the report that, “In three years, Nashville has successfully relocated over 500 people from eight outdoor encampments into permanent housing, interim housing or family reunification.”
This directly contradicts two previously published reports and statements from OHS.
Based on February data reported to Metro Council, 341 people resided in seven encampments that were closed.
And in a December sworn affidavit to a federal judge, OHS Director April Calvin wrote, “…
seven encampments across Davidson County have closed over the course of the last four years.
Those encampments had a total population of approximately five hundred residents,…”
I asked OHS whether there was an encampment closure of 100-150 people since February 2026 that I may have missed.
OHS answered that “The eight encampments referenced in the report include the Jefferson Street encampment.
The cumulative total covers a three-year period and does not indicate that an encampment of 100 to 150 people was closed between February and June 2026.”

The fact is that the Jefferson Street encampment could have been included in those previous reports since it was closed in early 2022 and certainly had far fewer than 100 people living there at the time of closure.
Unfortunately, these are not even close to all of the examples of contradictory, misleading and incorrect information I found in Metro’s 2026 State of Homelessness Community Report.
Everyone makes mistakes.

But to me, the consistency and continuity of the mistakes, even after being pointed out, strongly indicates that Metro homelessness leaders are more about elevating their own image than truly analyzing available data in an honest and transparent way that would allow us, as a community, to examine where we need to invest the millions of dollars that Metro continues to have at its disposal.
Metro Human Relations Commission Report Finds Probable Cause that OHS may have Discriminated Against Minorities
At the end of June, the Metro Human Relations Commission (MHRC) released an investigative report that examined a Title VI complaint against the Office of Homeless Services (OHS).
Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national origin in programs.

The MHRC report was extremely detailed and outlined the full accusation and essentially concluded that there is probable cause that OHS discriminated against people who belong to a minority population.

In his letter to OHS, his board, and others, MHRC Executive Director Davie Tucker wrote, “Based upon the Staff Investigative Report and my independent review, I hereby determine that there is probable cause to believe that the administration of federally funded housing assistance and housing stabilization programs by the Office of Homeless Services resulted in inconsistent application of policies and practices that had a disproportionate adverse effect on Black women and women of color, in a manner that warrants further proceedings under Rule 2.7 of the MHRC Rules and Procedures.
Accordingly, this complaint is upheld, and will advance to a formal conciliation process.”
Tucker’s letter also outlines a timeline that shows how unresponsive OHS was to requests from MHRC during this initial investigation.
The next step is conciliation, meaning that there will be a remediation attempt to eliminate the alleged discriminatory practice.

Tucker is also clear in his letter that “probable cause is not a finding of guilt, it is a higher standard than reasonable suspicion and demands a higher degree of certainty and fair probability that evidence of discrimination will be found.
Nothing in this Determination constitutes a final finding of discrimination or liability.”
Consumer Advisory Board (CAB) Payments RFP Now Open After Delay
When people in the human services field talk about paying people with lived experience for their participation, it is about acknowledging the value and expertise of these individuals.
Furthermore, people with lived experience and expertise often do not get paid for their time when we invite them to the table to solicit their input — while others are paid through their day jobs.

I asked OHS to help us understand why they stopped paying the Continuum of Care (Coc) Consumer Advisory Board (CAB) with the federal planning dollars, a direct grant from the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), that OHS receives on behalf of the community and that could be used for paying CAB members.

Here is the response, “When the Office of Homeless Services became the Collaborative Applicant for the Nashville Continuum of Care, Metro Charter provisions governing Metro Boards and Commissions applied to the Homelessness Planning Council and its committees.
As a result, OHS could no longer directly compensate individuals serving on those committees.

To establish a compensation process consistent with Metro requirements, OHS issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) to identify an independent organization to administer compensation for members of the Consumer Advisory Board (CAB) and Youth Action Board (YAB).”
After months of delays, that RFP is finally posted at https://www.nashville.gov/departments/office-homeless-services/continuum-care/current-rfp and open until July 31.
There is a lot of homelessness-specific terminology in the OHS statement that I won’t break down this time.
But as a former long-term Metro employee, I can confirm that Metro makes it very difficult to pay people with lived experience who sit on a board or on a committee.
In general, Metro, by law, cannot pay board/commission members.
The problem, however, is that in this instance:

• CAB members who asked for remediation of this situation for over a year did not request any payments for people sitting on the Homelessness Planning Council (HPC), which is the decision-making body of the Continuum of Care (CoC).
The CoC is composed of community stakeholders working together to build a homeless crisis response system.
• The HPC functions as the CoC Board and therefore, is a community board that happens to sit within Metro after it was combined with the Metropolitan Homelessness Commission in 2018.
But, the HPC is not your typical Metro board because the HPC has absolutely no power over Metro resources (neither the OHS budget, nor the final hiring or firing decision of HPC staff).
Their primary purpose is “to secure and manage federal funding, oversee the local homeless response system, and ensure compliance with HUD regulations.
• The only dollars over which the HPC has direct oversight are the Planning dollars managed by OHS as the Collaborative Applicant (a term the essential refers to the selected Lead Agency of the CoC).
• CoC committees, including the CAB and YAB, are not decision-making bodies as they only make recommendations to the HPC (see point 1).

My main question therefore is: how is it that Metro, including OHS, can hire multiple consultants through single-source contracts, but they cannot figure out what needs to be done to hire CAB and YAB members as independent contractors with the task to advise the HPC and the CoC?
Why All of This Matters
Taking a critical view of Metro’s approach to homelessness is necessary because the city is overseeing the largest funding pot ($18.5 million) to help some of our most vulnerable neighbors.
OHS touts to be data-driven.
But their data tells me they are output-driven and focus more on propaganda than using data for actual needs analysis.
I also believe that OHS has the potential because OHS has the resources at their disposal.
But OHS does not have the trust of the community or, seemingly, the will to build that trust.
We, as a city, can and should do better than what we have seen over the past few years.
Source documents, including the 2026 State of Homelessness Community Report and the two MHRC reports, will be linked to in our online version of this article.
Judith Tackett is a longtime homelessness expert and advocate for housing-focused, person-centered solutions.
Opinions in this column are her own.

Kristin Wilson has resigned as Metro's chief of operations and performance.

🦅 The best of the Banner in your inbox with The Flyer newsletter.
Metro’s chief of operations and performance Kristin Wilson is out at the mayor’s office after seven years.
Wilson joined Metro at the start of Mayor John Cooper’s term in 2019 and helped lead the city’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
She was retained when Mayor Freddie O’Connell took office in 2023.
Her responsibilities have included overseeing Metro department leaders.
Wilson previously was deputy chief operating officer for Atlanta and worked at a Nashville insurance company.
She resigned on Monday, according to the mayor’s office.
Her last day will be Aug.

In a resignation letter, Wilson wrote that she was grateful to Cooper and O’Connell and said it is time “to take a pause, to reflect on the work accomplished and my priorities for my career and life path going forward.”

“Though the work is not done, and as a city is always responding to changing needs of its constituents and many macroeconomic and existential contexts it does not control, it may never be fully complete,” Wilson wrote.

“But I do leave Metro believing it’s in a better operational place than it was when I started; that the leaders and employees of Metro have felt led, supported, challenged and recognized in ways I have directly contributed; and that the foundation for them to meet challenges and opportunities ahead is as strong as it has ever been.”
O’Connell has one year remaining in his term and publicly launched a reelection campaign this summer.
“I’m grateful to Kristin for her service to Metro over the last seven years,” O’Connell said in a statement.

“She has guided operations for two mayors, overseeing the city’s response to some of our most profound tragedies and crises while also guiding us through a considerable era of growth in our city that impacted operations.
Metro is better for her committed diligence.
Kristin has made the personal decision to resign, and I want to respect that.”
Key leaders remaining in the administration include chief of staff Masami Tyson , finance director Jenneen Reed and Choose How You Move chief program officer Sabrina Sussman.
Tyler Yarbro recently succeeded Wally Dietz as legal director.
Banner editor Steve Cavendish contributed to this story.

Key O’Connell Aide Steps Down From Nashville Mayor’s Office

by Stephen Elliott, Nashville Banner
August 18, 2026

Key O’Connell Aide Steps Down From Nashville Mayor’s Office

by Stephen Elliott, Nashville Banner
August 18, 2026

Metro's chief of operations and performance Kristin Wilson is out at the mayor's office after seven years. 

Wilson joined Metro at the start of Mayor John Cooper's term in 2019 and helped lead the city's response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

She was retained when Mayor Freddie O'Connell took office in 2023. 

Her responsibilities have included overseeing Metro department leaders.

Wilson previously was deputy chief operating officer for Atlanta and worked at a Nashville insurance company. 

She resigned on Monday, according to the mayor's office.
Her last day will be Aug.

28.

In a resignation letter, Wilson wrote that she was grateful to Cooper and O'Connell and said it is time "to take a pause, to reflect on the work accomplished and my priorities for my career and life path going forward."

"Though the work is not done, and as a city is always responding to changing needs of its constituents and many macroeconomic and existential contexts it does not control, it may never be fully complete," Wilson wrote.

"But I do leave Metro believing it's in a better operational place than it was when I started; that the leaders and employees of Metro have felt led, supported, challenged and recognized in ways I have directly contributed; and that the foundation for them to meet challenges and opportunities ahead is as strong as it has ever been." 

O'Connell has one year remaining in his term and publicly launched a reelection campaign this summer. 

"I'm grateful to Kristin for her service to Metro over the last seven years," O'Connell said in a statement.

"She has guided operations for two mayors, overseeing the city's response to some of our most profound tragedies and crises while also guiding us through a considerable era of growth in our city that impacted operations.
Metro is better for her committed diligence.

Kristin has made the personal decision to resign, and I want to respect that."

Key leaders remaining in the administration include chief of staff Masami Tyson, finance director Jenneen Reed and Choose How You Move chief program officer Sabrina Sussman.

Tyler Yarbro recently succeeded Wally Dietz as legal director.  

Banner editor Steve Cavendish contributed to this story.

The Metropolitan Government of Nashville-Davidson County Office of Homeless Services today released the certified results of the 2026 Point-in-Time Count, identifying 2,298 people (655 of 2,298 people unsheltered) experiencing literal homelessness on the night of Jan.
The annual count increased by 118 people, or 5.4%, from the 2025 Point-in-Time Count.
A requirement of the U.S.

Department of Housing and Urban Development, the count is one of the nation's primary tools for understanding homelessness at the local level and helps communities identify needs, monitor trends and inform decisions about housing, outreach, emergency shelter and supportive services.

More than 100 volunteers worked overnight alongside outreach teams, emergency shelter providers, health care partners, veterans’ organizations, nonprofit agencies and Metro staff to conduct this year's count.
Temperatures were already dangerously low on the night of the count, prompting Metro to activate its Cold Weather Plan and open the Metro Emergency Overflow Shelter.
The count also occurred several days before the onset of Nashville's most severe winter ice storm in decades.
Volunteers used their interactions to share shelter information and help people prepare for worsening conditions.
OHS continued coordinating with the Office of Emergency Management, Metro departments and community partners to help people get indoors and remain safe.
Nashville's PIT Count has fluctuated within a comparatively narrow range as homelessness increased substantially across the country and in similarly sized communities.
During the common 2022-2025 comparison period, Nashville's count increased 13.8%, compared with a 28% national increase and a 36.1% average increase among the selected comparison communities.
National and comparison-community data for 2026 have not yet been released.
Nashville's certified 2026 count was 2,298, a 5.4% increase from 2025.
Five-Year Trend

Mayor Freddie O'Connell had this to say:
The Point-in-Time Count provides an important snapshot of homelessness in Nashville and helps us better understand where needs exist across our community.
Behind every number is a person, and every person deserves the opportunity to access safe, stable housing.
I’m grateful to the volunteers, providers, health care partners and Metro staff who came together to make this year's count possible.
Their work helps us plan responsibly, make informed decisions and continue strengthening Nashville's response to homelessness.

Understanding the Point-in-Time Count
Communities across the country conduct the count during the same period each January.
Because the methodology remains consistent from year to year, the PIT Count provides an important benchmark for understanding trends over time.
The count includes people staying in emergency shelters, HUD-eligible transitional housing, people sleeping outdoors, or in places not meant for human habitation.
It is not a census of everyone who experiences homelessness during the year.

It does not include many individuals and families experiencing other forms of housing instability, such as people temporarily staying with friends or relatives or living in hotels or motels because of economic hardship.

What Was Different This Year
This year's results reflect the conditions present on the night of the count and several operational improvements that helped identify people experiencing homelessness more completely.
Metro's Cold Weather Plan and Emergency Overflow Shelter allowed more people to safely access emergency shelter that night.
Community partners expanded overnight outreach initiatives to engage individuals experiencing homelessness in every emergency department in Davidson County.

Health-focused outreach workers visited each emergency department twice during the overnight count to identify individuals who had not been admitted to the hospital but met HUD's eligibility requirements for inclusion in the Point-in-Time Count.
The count also included additional emergency shelter capacity by providers.

These new partnerships expanded the community's ability to identify people experiencing homelessness in locations that had not previously been incorporated into the overnight count, resulting in a more comprehensive and accurate snapshot of homelessness across Nashville.

April Calvin, Director of the Office of Homeless Services had this to say:
The data help us identify trends, evaluate needs, and work with our partners to strengthen the systems that connect people to housing and support.

We remain committed to collecting high-quality data, being transparent about what the data tell us, and using that information to make better decisions, strengthen our response, and achieve better outcomes for our community.
Who is Counted?

Category
Description

Unsheltered
People observed sleeping outdoors or in places not meant for human habitation.

Sheltered
People staying in emergency shelters designated for individuals experiencing homelessness.

HUD Transitional Housing
People staying in HUD-eligible transitional housing programs dedicated to individuals experiencing homelessness.

Who is NOT counted
This count does not include people who are doubled up with friends or family, living in hotels, or people staying in institutions such as jails or hospitals.

Why the Point-in-Time Count Matters
No single measure can fully capture the complexity of homelessness.
The Point-in-Time Count remains one of the most valuable tools available for understanding local needs, identifying trends and informing decisions about housing and services.

The Office of Homeless Services will continue working alongside nonprofit providers, health care organizations, outreach teams, volunteers, advocates and residents to strengthen Nashville's coordinated response to homelessness and expand pathways to safe, stable housing.

About the Office of Homeless Services
The Metropolitan Government of Nashville-Davidson County Office of Homeless Services leads Nashville's coordinated response to homelessness by aligning public investments, community partnerships, data, outreach, shelter, housing navigation and supportive services.

OHS works with nonprofit providers, health care partners, faith-based organizations, neighborhood groups, people with lived experience of homelessness and Metro departments to connect residents experiencing homelessness to resources that support housing stability.

The office also supports community planning, federal funding coordination, emergency response efforts, public information and systemwide strategies designed to improve outcomes for individuals and families.

Through transparent data, collaborative problem-solving and a focus on safe, stable housing, OHS helps Nashville make informed decisions and strengthen the community systems that serve neighbors experiencing homelessness.
